rooms.title: Ending the Game
rooms.description: Audience: readers who have played a few games of weiqi and are still unsure how a game actually ends, and why.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who have played a few games of weiqi and are still unsure how a game actually ends, and why.

Learning goal: explain what a [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) actually does, how players agree on dead stones, [dame](../../../glossary/terms/dame.md), and [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md) during the settlement phase, what happens when they disagree, how online servers automate the whole process, and why area and territory scoring almost always agree once settlement is done.

## Worked example: settling a disagreement under area scoring

Two players finish a 13x13 game under Chinese-style area rules. The board looks essentially decided: both sides have secured their frameworks, and neither has a move left that would gain more than it loses. Black passes. White passes. By the basic rule, two consecutive passes end the game and move both players into settlement, where they try to agree on which remaining groups are dead [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Here the disagreement shows up. White points at three Black stones sitting alone in the lower-left corner and calls them dead — surrounded, with no room to make two eyes. Black disagrees, convinced there is a hidden liberty that lets the group survive. Neither player has to win the argument. Because area scoring counts every living stone on the board plus enclosed territory, and does not charge either player extra for the stones needed to prove a point, they simply resume play: White plays into the corner to actually capture the group, and Black defends it as if the game had never stopped. Within a handful of moves the position answers its own question — either Black finds the second eye the group needed, or White finishes the capture — and the score reflects exactly what happened on the board, not what either player claimed [@polgote2026rules].

This is the moment that confuses almost every new player at some point: the game does not have a referee, a buzzer, or a rulebook check that fires automatically. "The game is over" is a claim two players make about the board, tested by passing, and if the claim does not survive the test, the players simply keep playing until it does. Understanding that passing is a claim, not a switch, resolves most of the confusion about when and why a game of weiqi ends.

## Passing signals "nothing here is worth a move"

A [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) is a player declining to place a stone on their turn. It is not a special move with its own effect on the board — it places nothing, so it is always legal, and it can never be blocked by the [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) rule or any other placement restriction, even while a ko fight is still open elsewhere on the board. It is, instead, a statement that, in the passing player's judgment, no move remains that would improve their position. Two consecutive passes — one from each player, in immediate succession — trigger the end of ordinary play and move both players into settlement [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

New players sometimes pass reflexively when they run out of obvious ideas, without checking whether any [dame](../../../glossary/terms/dame.md) remain unfilled or whether a marginal group is actually settled. Under scoring systems where filling dame is worth a point, an early pass can quietly hand that point to the opponent. Under scoring systems where dame are worth nothing either way, an early pass costs nothing but can still trigger settlement before a player intended it to, which is its own common surprise.

## The settlement phase: agreeing on dead stones

Once both passes land, the players do not immediately get a final score. They first attempt to agree on the status of every group still on the board: which stones are unquestionably alive, which are unquestionably dead, and which points are dame that belong to neither side [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. Stones both players agree are dead — hopeless strings that could not escape capture if play continued — are lifted off the board as prisoners without needing to be captured move by move. This is what makes settlement fast in the ordinary case: most games end with only one or two groups worth discussing, and the rest of the board is obvious to both players.

A group can also end up in a third state that is neither dead nor simply alive-and-settled: if two groups of opposite color are left sharing liberties that neither side can fill without immediately losing the resulting capturing race, the group is in [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md) — alive, but never awarded to either player as territory, under any ruleset. Seki stones are never removed during settlement; they simply stay on the board, unclaimed, for the rest of the game.

Settlement is an agreement, not a vote or a rule check. If both players agree a group is dead, it is treated as dead even though it was never actually captured. This is convenient, but it is also exactly the point where disagreement can surface.

## When players disagree: play it out

If the players cannot agree on a group's status, the rules do not ask them to argue further. They resume play. Under the AGA-style default rules that many Western clubs use, the opponent of whichever player passed last gets the next move, and the disputed group is fought out on the board exactly as in the worked example above. The game is over for real once the players reach agreement, or once both pass twice again in succession — at which point any stones still standing are simply ruled alive, disagreement or not [@britgo2025default].

Area scoring, described above, makes this resumption nearly free: every stone played toward proving a group dead or alive is still worth its normal value, so nothing is lost by actually playing out the fight [@britgoagaexplain2026]. This is also why Chinese-style area rules are often described as friendlier for beginners — there is less pressure to argue a disputed group correctly, because playing it out costs nothing extra.

### Japanese resumption rules, briefly

Classical Japanese rules handle the same problem with their own, stricter mechanism. Because territory scoring charges a player a point for playing an unnecessary stone inside their own territory, resuming play is not free the way it is under area scoring, so the rules are more careful about when a stopped game can be reopened. In the 1989 Japanese rules text, a player may request that a stopped game resume, and the opponent is obliged to allow it; the position is then played out and, once both sides again agree to stop, returned to what it would have been had the dispute never happened before the prisoners are counted [@swissgo2026japaneserules]. The text is also notably strict about bad-faith resumption: if a player later finds a move that would have gained something but the two players cannot agree whether the game should have already ended, the rules can rule that both players lose the game outright [@swissgo2026japaneserules]. Beginners rarely need this level of detail, but it explains why players coming from Japanese rules tend to be far more careful about exactly when they pass than players coming from area scoring.

## How online servers automate settlement

Go servers cannot rely on two people talking through a disagreement the way club players do, so they build the settlement phase directly into the interface. On the Online Go Server (OGS), for example, both passes move the game into a stone-removal phase: an automatic score estimator suggests which stones are dead, and each player can click stones to toggle them dead or alive and mark dame directly on the board [@ogs2026playinggames]. The automated suggestion is explicitly not meant to be trusted blindly — it is a starting point, not a ruling. Once both players accept the same result, the game locks in permanently; if they do not agree, either player can choose to cancel the settlement and resume play, which is the software version of the same resumption rule described above [@ogs2026playinggames]. Other servers vary in interface but follow the same shape: propose a settlement, let both sides correct it, and fall back to actual play when they cannot agree.

## Scoring the same board two ways

Once settlement is done — every group's status agreed or fought out, every dead stone removed — the game still needs to be turned into a final score, and the world's rulesets do this one of two ways. [Area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md) counts a player's living stones on the board plus that player's enclosed territory; it is what Chinese, AGA, New Zealand, and Ing rules use, and it is what the worked example at the top of this lesson assumed. [Territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md), used by Japanese rules, counts only a player's enclosed territory plus the prisoners captured from the opponent during play — stones sitting on the board earn no points of their own. The two methods count different things, but on a finished board where no captures happened during play, they tend to land on nearly the same margin between the players, once each ruleset's own standard [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md) is applied [@britgo2025default] — see the worked arithmetic in the [regression positions appendix](./regression-positions.md), which scores one small finished board both ways side by side.

## Why area and territory rarely differ

The two methods agree so often because of a simple accounting identity: for a finished position with no captures during play, a player's area score equals that player's territory score plus the number of that player's own stones sitting on the board. Since neither method credits a shared, neutral dame point to either side, the only way the two totals can diverge is if a player places a stone somewhere that changes one count without changing the other — concretely, by playing inside their own territory.

Playing inside your own territory is free under area scoring: the point simply stops being territory and starts being a stone, and the total stays the same. The identical move costs a full point under territory scoring, because the point stops being territory and nothing is gained to replace it. This is also why the two families of rules use slightly different standard komi values for what is meant to be a fair even game: because Black moves first, a finished game very often ends with Black having placed one more living stone than White, and area scoring credits that stone directly where territory scoring does not, so area-scoring rulesets typically set komi a point higher than territory-scoring rulesets covering the same game, exactly to offset this effect [@britgo2025default]. Where the two methods still differ by more than that fixed offset, the cause is nearly always a player filling their own territory unnecessarily, or a [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md) whose shared points the two methods treat identically but whose surrounding stones were counted differently along the way.

## Exercises

1. A player passes on move 140, then immediately regrets it because a large dame point is still open. Under area scoring, what does that pass cost them, and why would the same pass cost nothing under most forms of territory scoring?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Under area scoring, every stone on the board counts toward the final score, so leaving a fillable dame for the opponent to take is a real, one-point loss. Under territory scoring, dame are not counted at all — filling them establishes boundaries but does not add to either player's score — so passing before they are filled changes nothing about the count, even though it may still trigger settlement earlier than the player wanted.
</details>

2. Two players pass, then disagree about whether a five-stone group in the corner is dead. Under the AGA-style default rules, who gets to move first when play resumes, and what ends the game for good this time?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The opponent of whichever player passed last gets the next move. The game ends for good either when the players reach agreement on the group's status, or when both players pass twice again in succession, at which point any stones still on the board are simply ruled alive.
</details>

3. Why does an online server's "auto-score" or score-estimator button need a human override, instead of just deciding the game automatically?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Automated estimators are good at obvious cases but can misjudge close life-and-death situations, seki, or unusual dame configurations. Because the final result is often locked in permanently once accepted, servers let players correct the estimate — or cancel and resume play entirely — rather than trusting the automation to settle a genuinely disputed group.
</details>

4. Why doesn't a pass ever violate the ko rule, no matter what ko fights are active on the board?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because a pass places no stone and changes nothing about the board. The ko rule only restricts moves that would recreate a previous position; a pass cannot recreate anything, since it alters nothing.
</details>

5. A player fills one point of their own already-secure territory late in the game, capturing nothing. What happens to that player's score under area scoring, and under territory scoring?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Under area scoring the score is unchanged: the point simply converts from a territory point to a stone point, and both count the same. Under territory scoring the score drops by one point: the point stops counting as territory and nothing is gained in its place, since no capture occurred.
</details>

## What comes next

The next useful step is [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md), which explains what happens to the score that settlement produces here, or [Rulesets](./rulesets.md), which fixes exact komi, ko-regime, suicide, scoring, and handicap parameters for Chinese, Japanese, AGA, New Zealand, and Ing play, and the [regression positions appendix](./regression-positions.md), which works through small labeled positions — including both scoring methods — as concrete test cases. For the underlying vocabulary, continue with [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md), especially [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md), [dame](../../../glossary/terms/dame.md), [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md), [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md), [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md), [area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md), and [territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md).

rooms.title: Handicap Placement and Komi Values
rooms.description: Audience: readers who already understand the difference between komi and handicap and now need the operational tables: which hoshi to place in which order, what komi to use in a handicap game, standard even-game komi by ruleset, and the rank-to-stone conversion.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who already understand the difference between komi and handicap and now need the operational tables: which hoshi to place in which order, what komi to use in a handicap game, standard even-game komi by ruleset, and the rank-to-stone conversion.

Learning goal: place a fixed handicap of any size 2 through 9 in the standard order, choose the correct komi for a handicap or even game, and convert a rank gap between two players into a stone count.

This lesson assumes the conceptual distinction covered in [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md): komi is a scoring offset for an even game, handicap is a positional offset for an unequal one. Nothing here repeats that distinction. What follows is the operational layer: the tables a table director, a teacher, or an online server actually consults before a game starts.

## Worked example: setting up a game between a 5 kyu and a 1 kyu player

Two players want a fair game. One is 5 kyu, the other 1 kyu. The rank gap is four grades, so the rule of thumb calls for a four-stone handicap [@britgo2026rating]. The weaker player, 5 kyu, takes Black and places four stones before White's first move, on the four corner [hoshi](../../../glossary/terms/hoshi.md): the two diagonal corners used for a two-stone handicap, plus the third and fourth corners added in sequence [@wikipedia2026handicap]. Because this is a handicap game rather than an even game, White does not receive the usual 6 to 7 and a half point komi; instead, under Japanese rules (assumed here), the game is played at a nominal 0.5 komi, just enough to prevent a drawn result [@wikipedia2026komi]. Not every ruleset stops there — see the komi table below for the additional stone-scaled compensation Chinese and AGA rules add on top of that 0.5. If the two players later find the four-stone game one-sided, the standard adjustment is to change the stone count by one rather than to tune komi, since komi is calibrated for near-equal strength, not for large rank gaps.

## Standard placement order for fixed handicaps (19x19)

The nine hoshi are the 4-4 point in each corner, the 4-10 point at the midpoint of each edge, and the 10-10 center point (tengen). The Japanese fixed-placement tradition, which most rule sets treat as the default, adds stones in this order [@wikipedia2026handicap]:

| Stones | Points added | Points now on the board |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | two diagonal corners (upper right, lower left) | 2 corners |
| 3 | the third corner (lower right) | 3 corners |
| 4 | the fourth corner (upper left) | 4 corners |
| 5 | tengen (center) | 4 corners + center |
| 6 | the two side points, left and right; tengen is removed | 4 corners + 2 side points |
| 7 | tengen (center), added back | 4 corners + 2 side points + center |
| 8 | the remaining two side points, top and bottom; tengen removed again | 4 corners + 4 side points |
| 9 | tengen (center), added back | all 9 hoshi |

Two things about this table are easy to misread. Tengen is not cumulative: it appears at 5 and 7 stones, is absent at 6 and 8, and returns at 9. And a "one-stone handicap" is not a placement rule at all; giving Black the move order with no extra stone is simply an even game with Black already moving first, which is why the table starts at 2.

## Free placement in Chinese and Ing traditions

The fixed order above is the Japanese default, and it is also the AGA default. But it is not universal. Chinese, Ing (SST), and New Zealand rule sets let Black place the handicap stones on any points at all, not only the nine hoshi, and some of those rule sets add a small point compensation for the handicap stones on top of that free placement [@britgo2026compare]. The AGA rules keep the hoshi as the default but explicitly permit a tournament director to specify free placement instead [@britgo2026compare]. In practice this means the placement table above should be read as "the standard convention," not as a universal constraint: a director running an event under Chinese or Ing rules may legitimately allow Black to set the handicap stones anywhere on the board.

## Komi in handicap games

Once handicap stones are on the board, komi is no longer doing the job of compensating for the first-move advantage; the stones already overcompensate for that. Under Japanese, Ing (SST), and New Zealand rules, handicap games are played with a nominal komi of 0.5, present only to break what would otherwise be a tied score, not to offset anything structural [@wikipedia2026komi]. That flat 0.5 figure is not universal, though: Chinese and AGA rules additionally compensate White for the area the handicap stones occupy, on top of the same 0.5 tie-breaker. Under Chinese rules, for an *n*-stone handicap, *n*/2 is added to White's score and *n*/2 is subtracted from Black's; under AGA rules using area (Chinese-style) counting, *n*−1 is added to White's score instead [@britgo2026compare]. In every case this is a sharp departure from even-game komi, which runs into the mid-single digits, and it is the detail most often mishandled by newcomers running their own handicap games: raising handicap komi to even-game levels effectively hands White extra stones on top of the reduced handicap.

## Standard komi values by ruleset, and why they moved

Even-game komi has drifted upward across a century of play, and the drift is itself evidence about how large Black's first-move advantage actually is. Under Japanese rules, the Hisekai group used a 4.5 komi in 1922; the Oza tournament adopted 5.5 in 1955; and the Nihon Ki-in raised the Japanese-rules standard to 6.5 in 2002, citing a measured 51.855 percent win rate for Black under the old 5.5 figure as evidence the earlier komi undercompensated [@wikipedia2026komi]. Under American rules, the AGA moved from 5.5 to 7.5 komi in August 2004, effective in 2005 [@wikipedia2026komi]. Chinese-rules play used 5.5 for years before also settling on 7.5 as standard [@wikipedia2026komi; @britgo2026compare]. The British Go Association itself used Japanese rules with 6 or 6.5 komi for years before adopting AGA rules with 7.5 komi in 2007 [@britgo2026compare]. Ing rules use 8, and New Zealand rules use 7 [@britgo2026compare]. Current statistical estimates from professional and computer play put the value of Black's first move, under area scoring, at around 7 points [@wikipedia2026komi]. Read together, this history is not a story of arbitrary rule tinkering: each increase followed measured win-rate imbalance at the previous value, which is why the trend runs in one direction, from 4.5 up toward 7 or 7.5, rather than oscillating.

| Ruleset | Standard even-game komi |
|---|---|
| Japanese rules (current) | 6.5 |
| AGA rules | 7.5 |
| Chinese rules (current) | 7.5 |
| Ing (SST) rules | 8 |
| New Zealand rules | 7 |
| Japanese, Ing (SST), New Zealand rules, handicap games | 0.5 (nominal, breaks ties only) |
| Chinese rules, handicap games | 0.5, plus *n*/2 added to White and subtracted from Black for an *n*-stone handicap |
| AGA rules, handicap games (area counting) | 0.5, plus *n*−1 added to White for an *n*-stone handicap |

## The rank-gap rule of thumb

The simplest working rule for choosing a handicap size is that the number of handicap stones equals the difference in rank between the two players, one stone per full grade of separation, whether the grades are both kyu, both dan, or span the kyu-to-dan boundary [@britgo2026rating]. A 5 kyu playing a 1 kyu takes four stones, as in the worked example above. A 3 dan playing a 1 dan takes two stones. When the gap is exactly one grade, the common convention is to skip stones altogether and simply give the weaker player Black with no komi, rather than add a single handicap stone [@britgo2026rating]. This rule of thumb is deliberately coarse: it is a starting point for pairing unfamiliar players, not a guarantee of an even contest, and organizers routinely adjust the stone count by one after a session if the games it produces are consistently lopsided.

## Exercises

1. A 4 kyu player and a 9 kyu player want to play a handicap game under Japanese rules. How many stones, on which points, and what komi?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The rank gap is five grades, so Black takes a five-stone handicap: the four corner hoshi plus tengen (the center point). Komi is the nominal handicap value, 0.5, not an even-game komi.
</details>

2. A club is running a six-stone handicap game. A player new to handicap games assumes tengen must be one of the six points, since it appeared at five stones and will appear again at seven. Why is that assumption wrong?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Tengen is not cumulative across handicap sizes. It is added at 5 stones, removed at 6 (replaced by the two side hoshi), added back at 7, removed again at 8 (replaced by the remaining two side hoshi), and added back at 9. At six stones the board holds the four corners plus two side points, with no stone on tengen.
</details>

3. Why did the Nihon Ki-in raise Japanese-rules komi from 5.5 to 6.5 in 2002 instead of leaving it unchanged?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Recorded results under the 5.5 komi showed Black winning about 51.855 percent of games, indicating the existing komi undercompensated for the first-move advantage. Raising komi to 6.5 was a direct response to that measured imbalance, not an arbitrary change.
</details>

4. A tournament director running an event under Ing rules tells Black to "put the handicap stones wherever you like, not just on the hoshi." Is this an error?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

No. Ing rules, along with Chinese and New Zealand rules, permit free placement of handicap stones rather than requiring the fixed hoshi pattern. The Japanese fixed order is the common default, not a universal requirement.
</details>

## What comes next

For the conceptual groundwork this lesson builds on, return to [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md). For the board points these tables place stones on, see the glossary term [hoshi](../../../glossary/terms/hoshi.md), along with [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) and [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md). To connect handicap play back to ordinary game structure, continue with [Weiqi Overview](./weiqi-overview.md).

rooms.title: How Ranks Work
rooms.description: Audience: readers who have played a number of games and want to understand what their kyu or dan rank actually measures, how it relates to handicap stones, why it differs between organizations and servers, and what to realistically expect as their own rank moves.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who have played a number of games and want to understand what their kyu or dan rank actually measures, how it relates to handicap stones, why it differs between organizations and servers, and what to realistically expect as their own rank moves.

Learning goal: read a kyu/dan rank correctly, convert a rank gap into a handicap, explain why the same numeral means different things on different servers and in different countries, and know what normal rank progress looks like so early plateaus and losses stop feeling like evidence of failure.

## Worked example: two ranks, one number, three different meanings

A player's profile says "7 kyu." On its own that string tells you almost nothing portable. It tells you, roughly, how many stones that player would need from a much stronger opponent, and roughly how many stones they would give a much weaker one [@britgo2026rating]. It does not tell you how that player would fare against a 7 kyu on a different server, in a different country, or under a different organization's grading, because kyu and dan numbers are calibrated locally, not globally [@wikipedia2026goranks; @senseislibrary2026rankcomparison]. And if the "7 kyu" comes from an account with only a handful of games played, it may not even be a settled estimate of that player's own strength yet, only a provisional guess the rating system is still correcting [@kgs2026rank; @ogs2017glicko2]. All three of those facts are true about the same rank at once. This lesson takes them one at a time.

## The kyu/dan ladder

Weiqi ranks run in two connected but oppositely-ordered stretches. Beginners start somewhere in the 20s or 30s kyu (the exact starting point is a convention, not a law: the British Go Association's grading starts novices around 35 kyu) and improve by counting the kyu number *down* toward 1 kyu [@britgo2026rating; @wikipedia2026goranks]. Once a player is stronger than 1 kyu, the ladder switches direction: they become 1 dan and then count *up* through the amateur dan ranks, which run to 7 dan in most organizations and as high as 9 dan in a few [@wikipedia2026goranks; @britgo2026rating]. So the full amateur ladder, from weakest to strongest, reads roughly: 30 kyu, 29 kyu, ... 2 kyu, 1 kyu, 1 dan, 2 dan, ... 7 dan. There is no "0 dan" or "0 kyu" step; the ladder crosses directly from 1 kyu to 1 dan.

Professional dan ranks are a separate track, not a continuation of the amateur one. Professional 1 dan through 9 dan are awarded by national professional associations (in Japan, Korea, and China) based on tournament results and promotion examinations, and they are graded far more finely than amateur ranks: a professional 1 dan plays at roughly the level of a strong amateur 7 dan, and the entire spread from professional 1 dan to professional 9 dan corresponds to no more than two or three handicap stones of real strength difference [@britgo2026rating; @wikipedia2026goranks]. Treating "9 dan" as one uniform unit of strength across the amateur and professional tracks is the single most common misreading of the system: an amateur 9 dan and a professional 9 dan are not the same rank wearing the same label, and even within the professional track, the top ranks compress toward a narrow band of genuinely elite play rather than spreading out the way amateur kyu ranks do.

## Rank differences and handicap stones

Within a single organization's amateur ladder, the practical payoff of a rank is this: the number of handicap stones a weaker player takes from a stronger one is simply the size of the rank gap between them, counted in full grades, whether those grades are both kyu, both dan, or span the kyu-to-dan boundary [@britgo2026rating; @wikipedia2026goranks]. A few worked conversions:

| Stronger player | Weaker player | Rank gap | Handicap stones |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 kyu | 7 kyu | 4 | 4 |
| 5 kyu | 2 kyu | 3 | 3 |
| 4 dan | 1 dan | 3 | 3 |
| 4 dan | 4 kyu | 8 | 7 (capped near 9; see below) |

When the gap is exactly one grade, the usual convention is not to add a stone at all: the weaker player simply takes Black, which already carries the first-move advantage that komi would otherwise cancel [@britgo2026rating]. This one-stone-equals-no-extra-stone convention is why handicap tables typically start at two stones rather than one.

This rule of thumb holds reliably across single-digit kyu ranks and amateur dan ranks, which is exactly the range most players spend their time in [@wikipedia2026goranks]. It stops holding at the professional level, where, as noted above, a full eight-grade gap from professional 1 dan to professional 9 dan corresponds to only two or three stones of real strength, not eight [@wikipedia2026goranks; @senseislibrary2026rankcomparison]. Fixed handicap placement also has a practical ceiling: traditional board setups do not go past nine stones, so a rank gap larger than nine is not fully absorbed by stones alone. For the placement order itself and how komi changes in a handicap game, see [Handicap Placement and Komi Values](./handicap-placement-and-komi-values.md).

## Why the same number means different things in different places

Rank inflation and deflation is not a rumor players spread to feel better about losing; it is a documented, structural feature of how each organization sets its own promotion bar. A player who is judged 2nd kyu in one country may be judged only 5th kyu in another, purely because of how each system calibrates promotions, not because the player's actual skill changed when they crossed a border [@wikipedia2026goranks].

A few of the largest, best-documented gaps:

- **AGA (American Go Association).** The AGA's system is built on numerical ratings first; kyu/dan labels are a derived, informal translation layered on top, and the AGA does not issue amateur ranks above 7 dan [@senseislibrary2026rankcomparison]. Because AGA promotion at the kyu and low-dan levels is comparatively strict, AGA ranks in that range tend to run stronger-than-the-label, relative to more lenient systems [@wikipedia2026goranks].
- **EGF (European Go Federation).** The EGF also runs an explicit Elo-style rating underneath its ranks, but methodology and promotion practice vary noticeably between European national federations, so even "EGF rank" is not perfectly uniform across Europe [@senseislibrary2026rankcomparison].
- **Japanese and Korean associations (Nihon Ki-in, Hanguk Kiwon, and equivalents).** These are the oldest continuously operating grading bodies and issue both amateur and the professional dan ranks described above. Their amateur grading conventions predate the rating-system era and were set independently of AGA or EGF calibration, which is part of why cross-comparisons need an explicit conversion rather than a direct numeral match [@wikipedia2026goranks; @britgo2026rating].

None of this means rank is meaningless. Within one organization, on one ladder, the handicap correspondence above holds well. The caution is narrower and more specific: never assume a rank earned on one ladder transfers unchanged to another without checking how that other ladder is calibrated.

## Online servers: rank is relative to that server's own pool

Online servers add a further wrinkle. A server rank is a statement about where you sit inside that specific server's population of active players, not a portable statement about your strength on any absolute scale [@senseislibrary2026rankcomparison].

- **KGS** computes a player's rank by scanning the ranked games that player has played in roughly the last 180 days and deriving a rank from those results; a new account's rank displays with a "?" until it has accumulated wins against solidly-ranked opponents and losses against solidly-ranked opponents in both directions, at which point the provisional mark is dropped [@kgs2026rank]. KGS's own professional ranks are explicitly on a different scale from KGS's amateur kyu/dan ladder, which the server documents itself; KGS does not compute those pro ranks from game results at all, but simply displays the rank a player was already awarded by an outside professional Go organization such as the Nihon Ki-in or Hanguk Kiwon [@kgs2026rank].
- **Fox** is informally reported by players who hold ranks on both servers to run noticeably weaker at the same numeral than KGS, on the order of a couple of ranks [@lifein19x192026fox]. This kind of cross-server comparison is necessarily informal, built from players' lived experience of moving between servers rather than from a shared calibration, which is itself the point: there is no authority reconciling Fox's ladder against KGS's.
- **OGS (Online-Go.com)** moved to a Glicko-2 based rating system in 2017; ranks shown to players are derived from the underlying rating rather than being the primary number [@ogs2017glicko2]. Because OGS's rank is a function of its own rating pool, it is calibrated to OGS's own players, not to KGS, Fox, or any offline federation.

The practical upshot: comparing your rank across two servers, or between a server and an in-person club's grading, is a rough translation exercise, not a lookup. Treat any such comparison as an estimate good to a stone or two, not an exact equivalence.

## How modern servers actually derive your rank

Older systems, including the original Elo rating system built for chess, track a single number per player: a point estimate of strength that moves up after wins and down after losses, with the size of the move set by a fixed constant. That single number carries no explicit statement of how confident the system is in it.

The Glicko and Glicko-2 rating systems, which are public-domain and widely used on game servers including Online-Go.com, add exactly that missing confidence measure: a ratings deviation (RD), which behaves like a standard deviation around the point rating [@wikipedia2026glicko]. A newly created, unrated account starts with maximum uncertainty, typically an RD around 350, which shrinks as the account accumulates games against opponents whose own ratings are already well established [@wikipedia2026glicko; @ogs2017glicko2]. Glicko-2 goes one step further and also tracks a volatility term, which captures how erratically a player's results are moving, separately from the plain rating and its uncertainty [@wikipedia2026glicko].

This matters concretely for a beginner because servers use that uncertainty measure operationally, not just for display. OGS, for example, does not offer handicap games by default to players whose deviation is still high, precisely because a rank with a wide uncertainty band is not yet a reliable basis for setting a fair handicap [@ogs2017glicko2]. A "?" next to a KGS rank is the same idea expressed differently: the system is telling you, explicitly, that the number attached to your account is not yet a settled estimate [@kgs2026rank].

## What a beginner should actually expect

Put the last two sections together and a specific, reassuring picture falls out.

**Expect a fast early climb that is partly an artifact of the rating math, not proof of rapid skill gain.** While your account's uncertainty (RD) is still high, each game moves your rating a large amount, because the system is still resolving a wide range of plausible strength down to a narrower one [@wikipedia2026glicko; @ogs2017glicko2]. A brand-new player often shoots through several kyu ranks in their first weeks. That speed is real information resolving quickly, not a sign you are exceptionally talented, and it is expected to slow down.

**Expect plateaus, and do not read a plateau as failure.** As your uncertainty shrinks, each individual game result moves your rating less, by design [@wikipedia2026glicko]. Spending weeks or months at the same rank while you absorb harder material (life and death reading, whole-board judgment) is the system behaving exactly as intended: it has converged on a good estimate of your current strength, and moving that estimate now requires more accumulated evidence, not less effort from you.

**Expect to lose close to half your games once your rank is settled, and treat that as the healthy state, not a warning sign.** Rating and matchmaking systems are built on one principle: in an even game between two players of genuinely equal strength, each has a 50% chance of winning [@britgo2026krfaq]. Because ranked matchmaking tries to pair you against opponents near your own rank, a correctly calibrated rank should produce a win rate close to 50% against that pool, not close to 100% [@britgo2026krfaq]. If you are winning far more than half your games, your rank has not yet caught up with your actual strength and will rise; if you are losing far more than half, the reverse is true. A near-even record is not evidence you have stopped improving. It is evidence the number next to your name is currently accurate, which is the entire point of having one.

## Exercises

1. A player is 6 kyu and wants a handicap game against a friend who is 2 dan. How many handicap stones should the weaker player take?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The ladder runs ...4 kyu, 3 kyu, 2 kyu, 1 kyu, 1 dan, 2 dan. From 6 kyu to 1 kyu is 5 grades, and from 1 kyu to 2 dan is 2 more grades (1 kyu to 1 dan, then 1 dan to 2 dan), for a total gap of 7 grades. The weaker player takes 7 handicap stones.
</details>

2. A player holds a "5 kyu" account on one server and a "5 kyu" account on a different server, and loses most of their games when they use the second account against players who were also 5 kyu there. Does this mean the player's strength has gotten worse?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Not necessarily. Ranks are calibrated to each server's own player pool, and different servers are documented to run their ladders at different overall strengths (Fox running informally weaker than KGS at the same numeral is one concrete example). A rank that transfers unchanged in label can still sit at a different real strength on a different server, so a losing record right after switching servers is often a calibration gap, not a skill decline, until enough games let that account's own rating settle.
</details>

3. After ten games on a brand-new account, a player's rank has already moved by six grades, and then over the next two hundred games it moves by only two more. Is something wrong with the rating system?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

No. A new account starts with maximum rating uncertainty, so early games move the estimate a large amount as the system narrows down a wide range of plausible strength. As uncertainty shrinks with more games against well-established opponents, each additional result carries less new information and moves the rating less. Fast early movement followed by a slow, plateauing rate of change is exactly how an uncertainty-tracking rating system (Glicko/Glicko-2) is supposed to behave, not a sign of malfunction.
</details>

4. A player has stopped improving quickly and is now winning about half of their ranked games. Should they be discouraged?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

No. A correctly calibrated rank, matched against opponents near that same rank, is expected to produce a win rate close to 50%, since an even game between equally strong players gives each side about a 50% chance of winning. Winning close to half your games is the signature of an accurate rank, not a sign of stalled progress. Sustained improvement will show up as the rank itself moving upward over time, not as the win rate at any single rank climbing toward 100%.
</details>

## What comes next

For the operational tables this lesson assumes but does not repeat, continue with [Handicap Placement and Komi Values](./handicap-placement-and-komi-values.md), which covers exact stone placement order and the komi used once a handicap is set. For the underlying distinction between komi and handicap, return to [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md). For vocabulary, see the glossary terms [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) and [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md). For the broader structural picture this lesson sits inside, return to [Weiqi Overview](./weiqi-overview.md).

rooms.title: Ko and Superko
rooms.description: Audience: readers who already understand the simple ko rule and want to know why long cycles need a stronger rule, and how that stronger rule differs across rulesets.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who already understand the simple ko rule and want to know why long cycles need a stronger rule, and how that stronger rule differs across rulesets.

Learning goal: explain why simple ko is not enough to stop every repeating position, define positional and situational superko, and know which rulesets use which.

## Worked example: a cycle simple ko cannot see

Imagine three separate, interlocking ko fights on the board at once — call them ko A, ko B, and ko C. Black captures ko A. White, unable to retake ko A immediately, captures ko B instead. Black, unable to retake ko B immediately, captures ko C. White, unable to retake ko C immediately, retakes ko A — which is legal now, because ko A's capture happened three of White's moves ago, not one. Black then retakes ko B, and White then retakes ko C. After these six plies, the whole board is back to exactly the position it held before Black's first capture, and it is Black's turn again, exactly as it was then.

The [simple ko rule](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) never objected once during this sequence, because at every step the move in question recreated a position from several moves back, not the position from immediately before the opponent's last capture [@britgo2025default]. Nothing in simple ko stops the six of them from repeating this loop forever. This is a **triple ko**, and it is the clearest illustration of why weiqi rulesets need something stronger than simple ko.

## Simple ko: a quick recap

The [simple ko rule](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) forbids exactly one move: the immediate recapture that would recreate the board position exactly as it stood just before the opponent's last capture [@britgo2025default]. If White captures a single Black stone in a ko, Black cannot retake it on the very next move, because doing so would restore the position from one move-pair earlier. Black must play a [ko threat](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) elsewhere first, giving White a chance to respond or to connect the ko, before Black can try to retake it.

That rule is deliberately narrow. It looks exactly one move-pair into the past and no further. For an ordinary single ko, that is all that is needed — the only way to recreate the forbidden position quickly is the one banned recapture. But narrowness is also its limit.

## Why simple ko is not enough

Simple ko's one-move lookback cannot see a cycle whose period is longer than one move-pair. The triple ko above has a period of three move-pairs (six plies): the position that recurs was last seen three of the mover's own turns ago, not one, so the rule's test never triggers. The same blind spot applies to two other named patterns:

- **Eternal life** (chosei), a rotating capture-and-recapture pattern, often four to six plies long, in which players repeatedly sacrifice stones as ko threats and the position cycles back to an earlier state without either side gaining ground [@brouwer2026eternallife].
- **Sending-two-returning-one**, a shape (most often along an edge) where a player can sacrifice two stones and recapture only one, resetting the local position while technically making a different move each time, which lets the position on the whole board recur even though no single move looks like a repeat [@britgo2026compare].

All three patterns share the same structure: a position from earlier in the game recurs, but not from one move ago, so a rule that only checks one move back cannot stop it. Left unresolved, any of them can repeat without end, and the game cannot reach a score.

## Positional superko vs situational superko

Superko rules close this gap by checking a candidate move against the *entire history* of positions in the game, not just the immediately previous one. Two variants are in common use, and the difference is in exactly what counts as "the same position" [@jasiek2026superko]:

- **Positional superko**: illegal to play a move that would recreate any whole-board position that has occurred at any earlier point in the game — the stones on the board must never repeat, independent of whose turn it is to move.
- **Situational superko**: illegal to play a move that would recreate a position that occurred earlier in the game *with the same player to move next*. If the identical stone arrangement occurred before but it was the other player's turn, replaying it is legal.

Applied to the triple ko above, both variants agree: the position White or Black would be recreating at ply six is identical in stone arrangement *and* in whose turn is next (the cycle's period is even, so the same player is always to move at the recurrence), so both positional and situational superko forbid the repeating move and force one side to break the cycle by playing elsewhere. Cases that actually distinguish the two variants — where the arrangement of stones repeats but with the opposite player to move — exist but are rare enough in practice that Jasiek's comparative study of the two finds "the actual difference... as to occurring positions is rather small" [@jasiek2026superko]. The variants matter more for how a rule is *written and proven correct* than for how often they produce different outcomes at the board.

## Which rulesets use which

| Ruleset | Approach to long cycles |
|---|---|
| AGA (American Go Association) | Explicit situational superko: a move may not recreate a board position from earlier in the game with the same player to move [@britgo2026agasummary]. |
| New Zealand | Adopted positional superko in 1975, closely modeled on the Taiwanese (Ing) rule text, then switched to situational superko in 1978 [@jasiek2026superko]. It is often grouped with the positional-flavored rulesets because of that shared textual lineage even in its current situational form. |
| Ing (Taiwan) | Does not state a single blanket superko clause. Instead it separates "fighting kos" from "disturbing kos" and restricts repetition of position within each category on positional grounds — same board content, not same player to move — which gives it a positional flavor without adopting positional superko as one general rule [@jasiek2026superko]. |
| Chinese | The written rule (1988) states a positional-style prohibition on repeating any board position [@jasiek2026superko]. In tournament practice, however, complicated repetitions such as triple ko are often simply ruled void rather than resolved by that clause, and many Chinese tournaments prohibit the sending-two-returning-one shape outright rather than leaning on superko to police it [@britgo2026compare]. |
| Japanese | Does not generalize ko into a superko rule at all. The ko rule covers only the ordinary single-stone case. When a longer cycle such as triple ko or eternal life arises and neither player will give way, the game is declared "no result" (or void) and is normally replayed [@britgo2026compare; @brouwer2026tripleko; @brouwer2026eternallife]. |

The pattern across all five: everyone agrees simple ko is insufficient, but they disagree on the fix. AGA and (currently) New Zealand write a superko clause into the rules and let it silently absorb triple ko, eternal life, and sending-two-returning-one as special cases of one general principle. Chinese rules write a similar clause but often fall back on Japanese-style voiding in practice. Japanese rules never generalize the clause at all, treating every long cycle as an exceptional outcome for the tournament director rather than an illegal move for the rules engine to reject.

## What this means in practice for online play

A server that only labels its ruleset "Japanese," "Chinese," or "AGA" has not actually told a player (or a rules engine) what happens the one time in a thousand games that a long cycle appears — that behavior depends on which superko variant, if any, sits underneath the named ruleset. This is not a hypothetical concern: in KGS's computer Go tournaments, the server enforced positional superko strictly, and the report on that period found several games where a program's intended move was illegal only under positional superko and would have been permitted under situational or natural situational superko — in a few cases deciding the outcome when a program, unable to find a legal alternative, timed out or played badly instead [@kgs2026superko]. Positional superko is also the stricter of the two common variants: it forbids some positions that situational superko would allow, since it does not exempt a repeat where the player to move differs.

For a human game between casual players, the choice of superko variant almost never matters — long cycles are uncommon, and the two variants virtually never diverge on the position actually reached. It matters for exactly the audiences this distinction was built for: rules engines and tournament software that must decide, without a human referee in the room, whether a candidate move is legal; and any platform serving multiple named rulesets, which has to pick a concrete superko variant (or none, plus a no-result path) for each one rather than leaving it implicit.

## Exercises

1. Why does the simple ko rule fail to stop a triple ko, even though it reliably stops an ordinary single ko?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Simple ko only forbids recreating the position from exactly one move-pair ago. A triple ko's repeating position last occurred three move-pairs earlier, well outside that one-move lookback, so the rule's test never triggers even though the same position keeps recurring.
</details>

2. A move would recreate a board position that occurred earlier in the game, but the player to move next is the opposite of who was to move next at that earlier occurrence. Is the move legal under positional superko? Under situational superko?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Illegal under positional superko, which bans any recurrence of the whole-board arrangement regardless of whose turn it is. Legal under situational superko, which only bans a recurrence when the same player is to move next — here the player to move is different, so situational superko does not object.
</details>

3. Under Japanese rules, what happens if a triple ko appears and neither player is willing to break the cycle?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The game is declared "no result" (void) rather than decided, and is typically replayed, since Japanese rules do not generalize the ko rule into a superko clause that would forbid the repeating move outright.
</details>

## What comes next

For the underlying vocabulary, see [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) and [superko](../../../glossary/terms/superko.md) in the glossary, along with [capture](../../../glossary/terms/capture.md) and [liberty](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md). For how the same superko question fits alongside scoring style, standard komi, and suicide across named rulesets, see [Weiqi Rulesets](./weiqi-rulesets.md). For the broader structural picture that ko and superko sit inside, continue with [Living Groups and Eyes](./living-groups-and-eyes.md). For how rulesets diverge on scoring rather than repetition, see [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md).

rooms.body:
Audience: readers who understand basic weiqi structure and want to know how even games and uneven games are balanced.

Learning goal: explain the difference between komi and handicap, and show why weiqi uses both.

## Worked example: even game versus teaching game

In an even game, Black moves first and White receives [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md), a fixed score bonus that offsets the first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo]. In a teaching game between players of unequal strength, the weaker player may instead receive [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) stones before play begins [@britgo2026whatisgo]. These two adjustments solve different problems. Komi balances the initiative inside an otherwise equal game. Handicap balances the starting position between unequal players.

## Why komi exists

Weiqi is not fully symmetrical at the start because Black moves first [@britannica2026go; @britgo2026whatisgo]. Komi compensates for that structural advantage by adding points to White's final score. This means the core rules of play stay the same while the scoring system absorbs the asymmetry.

Komi therefore belongs to scoring, not to local tactics. It matters when the final [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md) and related points are counted, not when players are reading captures or life-and-death fights.

## Why handicap exists

Handicap solves a different problem. It lets players of unequal strength compete in a game that still produces meaningful decisions for both sides [@britgo2026whatisgo]. Instead of changing how stones move or how groups live, handicap changes the starting position by placing extra Black stones on the board before the first move.

This matters pedagogically as well as competitively. A weaker player can experience middle-game and endgame decisions from a stronger position without needing the rules themselves to change.

## Komi and handicap are not interchangeable

Komi is a scoring offset in an even game. Handicap is a positional offset in an uneven game. They should not be collapsed into one idea just because both are balancing devices [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo].

The difference matters because each adjustment shapes play differently. Komi leaves the opening empty and symmetrical except for move order. Handicap creates immediate whole-board structure before ordinary play begins.

## Exercises

1. Why does komi affect the end of the game rather than the start of the board position?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because komi is a score adjustment, not an extra stone or changed move rule. It offsets Black's first move by changing the final count, not by altering local tactical play.
</details>

2. Why is handicap useful even though komi already exists?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because komi balances even games, while handicap balances games between players of different strength. They address different asymmetries.
</details>

## What comes next

The next useful step is to return to [History of Weiqi](./weiqi-history.md) for institutional context or to the local [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md), especially [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md), [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md), and [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md).

rooms.body:
Audience: readers who already understand liberties, capture, territory, and ko.

Learning goal: explain why connection and eye shape determine whether a group lives or dies.

## Worked example: a corner group with two eyes

Imagine Black has enclosed a small corner group so that two separate empty points remain inside its shape. White surrounds the outside completely. Even so, Black's group is usually safe. White cannot simply fill both internal points in sequence, because each point functions as an [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md), and the group remains alive as long as those internal liberties stay structurally separate [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

This example shows why raw stone count is not enough. A surrounded group can still live if its shape is strong enough. In weiqi, survival depends less on "having many stones" than on building a form that the opponent cannot legally or efficiently eliminate.

## Connection makes groups stronger

A [connection](../../../glossary/terms/connection.md) turns separate stones into one unit. That matters because connected stones share [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md), answer attacks together, and can build internal shape more efficiently than isolated stones can [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. Many local fights are therefore really fights over cutting and connecting.

When a player connects two weak stones, the move may look passive. But it often changes the status of the whole position. A connected group may escape [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md), threaten to make eyes, or stop the opponent from splitting the board into easy targets.

## Eyes and life

An eye is a protected empty point inside a group's shape. Under common rules, the opponent cannot simply play into a true eye if that move would leave the played stone without liberties and capture nothing [@britgo2025default]. That is why eye shape matters so much.

The usual practical rule is simple: a group with two secure eyes lives, while a group that cannot make two eyes may die [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. This is the core of [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md). Players read local sequences to determine whether a group can form those eyes before the opponent seals it in.

## Why this matters for the whole board

Life-and-death judgment is not a narrow endgame skill. It changes strategic value across the whole board. A move that saves a living group can preserve a large territorial framework. A move that kills an invading group can turn a contested region into secure [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md).

This is why advanced weiqi still returns to local shape. Whole-board strategy decides where to fight, but life-and-death reading decides whether the stones in that fight can remain on the board.

## Exercises

1. Why is a connected group usually stronger than the same stones scattered apart?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Connected stones share liberties, defend each other, and can build eyes as one unit. Scattered stones can be cut apart and attacked separately.
</details>

2. Why does the phrase "two eyes live" matter more than raw stone count?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

A group survives by preserving secure internal liberties, not by merely having many stones. Two proper eyes usually make capture impossible under ordinary play.
</details>

## What comes next

The next useful step is historical context in [History of Weiqi](./weiqi-history.md), then scoring structure in [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md), then continued vocabulary study through [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md), especially [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md), [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md), and [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md).

rooms.title: Obsmetrologia and Go Strategy
rooms.description: Audience: researchers and future sessions. Findings of the 2026-08-19 board-posed inquiry into whether Obsmetrologia contributes potentially novel Go strategy space: two surviving candidates, six rejections, and falsification paths. Questions and candidate structures, not results. Worked positions deliberately deferred.
rooms.body:
# Obsmetrologia and Go Strategy

The board asked: *is there anything the Obsmetrologia mathematics contributes to the strategy of Go that is potentially novel and opens new Go strategy spaces?* An Opus investigator studied the Obsmetrologia corpus (the Lean library's Site/Sheaf/Cohomology stack, pymetrologic's theorem ledger, and seven research notes), the weiqi corpus and kernel, and the actual state of Go theory — Berlekamp–Wolfe combinatorial game theory, thermography and miai counting, and engine-era ownership analysis, with literature checks rather than memory. Eight candidate bridges were assessed. Two survived; six did not.

This note records the findings so they are not re-derived. It deliberately contains **no worked positions**: constructing and verifying candidate positions is deferred until the weiqi content checker (weiqi-lsp) can machine-verify diagrams, and until someone chooses to extend this inquiry. Everything below is conjecture and is labeled as such.

## Surviving candidate 1 — Coordination cohomology as an obstruction to whole-board decomposability

Berlekamp–Wolfe endgame theory draws its power from treating a position as a disjunctive sum of independent local games; it has no formal device for a single move whose effect is shared across otherwise-independent regions — a ladder-breaker serving two ladders, a stone that is aji for two separate fights. When decomposition fails, the theory stops applying rather than quantifying the failure, and engine evaluation, being monolithic, does not localize it.

`Obsmetrologia/Cohomology/CoordinationCohomology.lean` proves, for its federated-cover domain, that the cover nerve's Ȟ¹ = |E| − |V| + |C| counts exactly the cells in excess of a spanning forest — the irreducible cross-region coordination. **Conjecture:** building the analogous nerve from Go regions (vertices) and shared-effect points (edges) yields a localized, computable measure of *how much, and exactly where, whole-board reading rather than regional reading matters* — a formalization of "whole-board vision" that neither CGT, classical thickness/aji heuristics, nor engine evaluation expresses. Literature search found no existing sheaf-theoretic or cohomological treatment of Go decomposability.

**Falsification path:** once the platform's engine review service exists (platform plan, Phase 3), compute the nerve's cycle rank over positions from real games and test whether it predicts where region-local analysis and whole-board engine analysis disagree. No correlation kills the idea.

## Surviving candidate 2 — The inconsistency sheaf as a formalization of aji

Aji is latent potential whose resolution depends on context not yet played — a local-to-global compatibility question. `Obsmetrologia/Cohomology/InconsistencySheaf.lean` (on `Site/Section.lean` and `SettlingCohomologyH1.lean`) formalizes a structured object carrying evidence-for and evidence-against separately, with restriction maps and an explicit gluing obstruction. Applied to a contested group's status across read-lines or assumed future contexts, this differs in kind from KataGo's shipped per-point ownership standard deviation and score variance, which are scalar sampling statistics. **Conjecture:** the obstruction class distinguishes two things engines blur — *"this resolves with deeper reading"* (the obstruction vanishes as settling proceeds) from *"this structurally depends on undetermined context elsewhere on the board"* (the obstruction persists) — and the second is aji, captured as a formal object. No paraconsistent-logic-for-Go or sheaf-theory-for-Go literature was found.

**Falsification path:** correlate a computed obstruction measure against engine review data — cases where deeper search changes a local status assessment versus cases where it does not. If obstruction persistence fails to track context-dependence, the idea dies.

## Rejected candidates, with reasons

- **Sheaf-gluing as miai** — miai's operative content (equal counting value) is already fully captured by established miai counting; the germ-preorder vocabulary restates it without new predictive content.
- **Chu-space / concurrent-game semantics for sente and gote** — the corpus's own 2026-06-18 note derives Conway's CGT as the finite/agon regime of the same category, i.e. the machinery is presented as subsuming existing theory, not exceeding it.
- **Occupation entropy as whole-board heat** — the Boltzmann multiplicity over occupation counts collapses onto what KataGo's ownership variance and CGT's temperature already expose.
- **Germ orders / antisymmetry-thinness as settledness** — real, machine-checked mathematics, but proof-architecture hygiene (relevant to building candidate 2 correctly), not itself a strategic claim.
- **Transfinite regime tower as a reading-depth axis** — Go is finite, perfect-information, chance-free; the whole game sits at one point of the tower, and finite complexity theory (PSPACE/EXPTIME results) already covers settling hardness.
- **Caillois four-regimes reading of Go's phases** — vocabulary import onto standard phase theory with no new evaluative content.

## Status and next steps

Both surviving candidates are analogies with construction sketches, not results. The natural next step, if the board chooses to fund it, is a single worked-position study per candidate — authored only once weiqi-lsp can verify the diagrams mechanically — followed by the Phase 3 falsification experiments above. The full investigator's report, including per-file study notes, exists in the 2026-08-19 session record.

rooms.title: Provenance Policy
rooms.description: Audience: contributors and agents editing weiqi-services-section content. States the one provenance convention this section uses, replacing the ad hoc date-suffixed-sibling and inline-import conventions found in earlier work.
rooms.body:
# Provenance Policy

Audience: contributors and agents editing weiqi-services-section content.

Learning goal: know where a historical or superseded copy of a document belongs, and how to mark it, without inventing a new convention per artifact.

## The policy

1. **Live documents are singular.** Every content item (lesson, term, topic, specification) has exactly one live copy at its canonical path under `content/`. Live documents never carry a date-suffixed sibling (no `<name>--archive-YYYY-MM-DD.md` next to `<name>.md`) and never carry a `--preexisting-*` sibling. If an older version of a live document is worth keeping, it moves — it does not stay parked next to the live copy.

2. **Imported or superseded copies live under `recovered-research/`.** Each content-type directory that needs one gets its own `recovered-research/` subdirectory, sibling to the live content it holds history for (for example `content/text/documents/articles/recovered-research/` for articles, `content/text/glossary/recovered-research/` for glossary terms). A file lands there when it is: an externally-imported historical draft that predates the live document, or a superseded version retired in place of an edited live document.

3. **Every file under `recovered-research/` carries a `provenance:` frontmatter field.** The field is a short prose string stating what the file is, where the live copy now lives (a relative link), and why it was retired — enough for a future reader to know this is not the current source of truth without opening both files. Example:

   ```yaml
   provenance: "Archived copy of the atari glossary term as it stood before the 2026-08-17 revision; superseded by ../../terms/atari.md, which is a strict superset (adds Related terms and full frontmatter). Retained for corpus history only — do not link to this file from live content."
   ```

4. **Nothing outside `recovered-research/` gets a `provenance:` field.** Live documents are trusted as current by default; provenance bookkeeping is only needed where a reader could otherwise mistake an old copy for the live one.

## Why one policy

The predecessor session that did this corpus's provenance work left four inconsistent conventions in play at once (recovered-research directories, `--archive-DATE` siblings, `--preexisting-glossary` siblings, and inline imported-source blocks) — exactly the "corpus hygiene debt" the platform plan names as a Phase 0 blocker (see [Weiqi Platform Plan](./weiqi-platform-plan.md), "Knowledge architecture and content operations," item 2). A single policy means a contributor never has to guess which convention applies to a given file, and a script never has to special-case four shapes to find the live copy of anything.

## Applying this policy retroactively

As of 2026-08-19, this policy was applied to the term-level `--archive-2026-08-17` siblings left in `content/text/glossary/terms/`: each was compared against its live sibling, confirmed to add no content the live copy lacked, and moved to `content/text/glossary/recovered-research/` under its plain term name with a `provenance:` field added. The pre-existing lesson duplicates in `content/text/documents/articles/recovered-research/` (already correctly located) were likewise given `provenance:` fields for consistency, since they predated this policy and lacked the field.
