rooms.title: Regression Positions
rooms.description: Audience: kernel implementers. Thirteen small, hand-verified board positions, each labeled with an expected outcome, meant to seed the rules kernel's regression test corpus.
rooms.body:
Audience: kernel implementers building `@lenticule-science/weiqi-kernel`, per the [Weiqi Platform Plan](./weiqi-platform-plan.md)'s call for "a corpus of regression positions drawn from the rules-completeness documents so the doctrine and the code cite each other."

Learning goal: give the kernel a first, hand-checked set of small positions covering ko, superko, suicide, seki, dead-stone settlement, both scoring methods, and handicap placement — each with a stable id and an expected outcome precise enough to assert against in a test file.

## Diagram format

Every diagram below is a complete, self-contained board of the exact size stated — not a fragment of a larger board — so every edge shown is a true board edge and every liberty count is unambiguous. Columns are lettered left to right starting at `A`; rows are numbered top to bottom starting at `1`. Symbols: `X` = Black stone, `O` = White stone, `.` = empty point, `*` = an empty point of particular interest (a ko point, or the point about to be played), called out in the prose beneath each diagram. Coordinates are written column-then-row, e.g. `B2`.

Each position carries an `id` for citation from kernel test files, and an `expected:` block giving the outcome as key-value pairs, matching the [rulesets](./rulesets.md) identifier vocabulary where applicable.

## R1 — simple ko: retake illegal

```
    A B C D E
  1 . . . . .
  2 . . X . .
  3 . X * X .
  4 . O X O .
  5 . . O . .
```

5×5 board. Black's last move was `C4`, which captured a lone White stone that had been sitting at `C3` (White's only liberty was `C4`, since `B3`, `D3`, and `C2` were already Black). It is now White's turn.

```
expected:
  id: R1-simple-ko
  ko_point: C3
  white_may_play_C3: illegal
  reason: >
    Playing C3 would capture Black's single stone at C4 (its only liberty is
    C3) and would recreate, point for point, the whole-board position that
    existed immediately before Black's last move. Forbidden under simple ko
    and under every ruleset in this corpus, since simple ko is their shared
    baseline. White must play elsewhere first.
```

## R2 — positional superko: a long cycle simple ko alone would permit

Take the shape at R1, but suppose the surrounding position also contains a second, independent ko elsewhere on the board (structurally identical to R1's shape, at points `K1`/`K2` rather than `C3`/`C4`). A well-known property of two independent, alternately-played ko fights is that captures and recaptures can, after several plies, return the *entire* board to an exact earlier arrangement while it is again the same player's turn to move — this is the standard "long cycle" (triple-ko-style) case rules literature uses to motivate superko.

```
expected:
  id: R2-positional-superko-long-cycle
  reason: >
    Simple ko only inspects the single position immediately before the
    opponent's last move, so it does not by itself forbid a position from
    recurring several plies later. Positional superko forbids the move that
    would recreate ANY position that has occurred earlier in the game,
    regardless of whose turn it was then, so it forbids this recurrence
    where simple ko alone would not.
  note: >
    Given here as a structural specification, not a fully hand-traced move
    list: the exact intervening sequence should be constructed and verified
    directly against the kernel's board history once superko is
    implemented, using two instances of the R1 ko shape as the starting
    point.
```

## R3 — situational superko permits what positional superko forbids

Using the same long-cycle setup as R2: suppose the identical whole-board position recurs, but with the *opposite* player to move compared to its earlier occurrence (an odd number of stone-placing plies apart, rather than an even number).

```
expected:
  id: R3-situational-superko-permits
  reason: >
    Positional superko forbids this recurrence outright, since it inspects
    the board only, not whose turn it is. Situational superko permits it,
    because SSK's forbidden unit is the pair (position, player-to-move), and
    here the player to move differs from the earlier occurrence — so under
    ruleset.aga (situational superko) this move is legal, while under
    ruleset.chinese, ruleset.newzealand, and ruleset.ing (positional
    superko) the equivalent move is illegal.
  note: >
    Given here as a structural specification alongside R2, for the same
    reason; verify the exact parity of the intervening plies against the
    kernel's implementation before relying on this as a literal test fixture.
```

## R4 — suicide: illegal under standard rulesets

```
    A B C
  1 X X X
  2 X * X
  3 X X X
```

3×3 interior fragment; treat the Black ring shown as having additional liberties outside this diagram on a larger board, so it is unconditionally alive and unaffected by White's move. It is White's turn, considering `B2`.

```
expected:
  id: R4-suicide-illegal
  white_may_play_B2: illegal (under ruleset.chinese, ruleset.japanese, ruleset.aga, ruleset.ing)
  reason: >
    B2's four neighbors are all Black. Black's ring is alive (liberties
    exist outside this fragment), so White's stone at B2 would capture
    nothing and would itself have zero liberties: suicide.
```

## R5 — suicide: legal only under New Zealand rules

Same diagram and same move as R4 (`B2`, all four neighbors Black, capturing nothing).

```
expected:
  id: R5-suicide-legal-nz
  white_may_play_B2: legal (under ruleset.newzealand only)
  result_if_played: >
    White's stone at B2 is placed and immediately removed as a self-capture
    (ruleset.newzealand.suicide = legal), per rulesets.md. Under every other
    ruleset in this corpus the same move is illegal — see R4.
```

## R6 — seki: minimal two-liberty standoff

```
    A B C
  1 X . O
  2 X . O
```

3×2 board (both edges shown are true board edges). Black group `{A1, A2}` and White group `{C1, C2}` each have exactly two liberties, `B1` and `B2`, both shared with the opponent. Neither group has an eye.

```
expected:
  id: R6-seki-minimal
  status: seki
  reason: >
    If either side plays B1 or B2, that side's own group drops to a single
    shared liberty while the opponent's group does too, and it becomes the
    opponent's turn — who then captures by playing the last shared point.
    Filling first therefore loses the group that fills. Neither side plays;
    both groups remain on the board for the rest of the game.
  scoring:
    territory: B1 and B2 count for neither player under ruleset.*.scoring = territory
    area: Black area = 2 (A1, A2 only), White area = 2 (C1, C2 only); B1
      and B2 count for neither player under ruleset.*.scoring = area, since
      they are not enclosed by one color alone.
```

## R7 — dead stones: unconditionally dead, no escape available

```
    A B C D
  1 X X X X
  2 X O * X
  3 X X X X
```

4×3 board, fully enclosed. White's single stone sits at `B2`; its only remaining liberty is `C2`.

```
expected:
  id: R7-dead-stone-no-escape
  status: dead
  white_group: [B2]
  reason: >
    White's only liberty is C2. If White plays C2 to try to gain space, the
    resulting two-stone White group (B2, C2) has zero liberties (every
    neighbor of both points is Black) and captures nothing: that move is
    itself illegal suicide. White therefore has no legal move that improves
    this group's status; it can never escape or make two eyes and is
    unconditionally dead. It may be removed during dead-stone settlement
    (see dead-stones.md) without either player needing to play out a
    capture.
```

## R8 — a legal capturing move is not suicide

```
    A B
  1 O *
  2 X .
```

2×2 board. White's stone at `A1` has exactly one liberty, `B1`. `A2` is Black; `B2` is empty. It is Black's turn, considering `B1` (marked `*`).

```
expected:
  id: R8-capture-not-suicide
  black_may_play_B1: legal
  reason: >
    Playing B1 removes White's last liberty at A1, capturing it. Captures
    are resolved before the mover's own liberties are checked, so even
    though B1's only other neighbor before the capture was White, Black's
    new stone gains a liberty at A1 the instant White's stone is removed
    (and already had one at B2). This is an ordinary capture, not suicide.
```

## R9 — area score of a finished board

```
       A B C D E F G
    1  . . X . O . .
    2  . . X O O . .
    3  . . X . O . .
    4  . . X X O . .
    5  . . X . O . .
```

7×5 finished board. Black wall at column `C` (5 stones) plus one extra move at `D4` filling a neutral point; White wall at column `E` (5 stones) plus one neutral-point fill at `D2`. Columns `A`–`B` are Black's territory (10 empty points, bordered only by the Black wall and the board edge). Columns `F`–`G` are White's territory (10 empty points, bordered only by the White wall and the board edge). `D1`, `D3`, `D5` are neutral points left unfilled, each bordered by both colors. No captures occurred during the game.

```
expected:
  id: R9-area-score
  ruleset: chinese
  black_stones_on_board: 6   # C1-C5, D4
  black_territory: 10        # A1-A5, B1-B5
  black_area_score: 16
  white_stones_on_board: 6   # E1-E5, D2
  white_territory: 10        # F1-F5, G1-G5
  white_area_score: 16
  white_final_with_komi: 23.5   # 16 + ruleset.chinese.komi (7.5)
  margin: White by 7.5
```

## R10 — territory score of the same finished board

Same diagram as R9. No captures occurred at any point during the game (prisoners for both players are zero).

```
expected:
  id: R10-territory-score
  ruleset: japanese
  black_territory: 10
  black_prisoners: 0
  black_territory_score: 10
  white_territory: 10
  white_prisoners: 0
  white_territory_score: 10
  white_final_with_komi: 16.5   # 10 + ruleset.japanese.komi (6.5)
  margin: White by 6.5
```

Note the raw totals (16–16 area vs. 10–10 territory) look different, but once each ruleset's own standard komi is applied the margins are close (7.5 vs. 6.5) — see R11 for the case where a wasted move inside one's own territory pushes them further apart, and see [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md#why-area-and-territory-rarely-differ) for why.

## R11 — where area and territory actually diverge

Start from R9/R10's finished position, then suppose Black plays one additional, unnecessary stone at `A3` — a point that was previously part of Black's own territory — before passing. Nothing is captured.

```
expected:
  id: R11-area-territory-diverge
  change_from_R9_R10: "Black plays A3 (own territory) before passing; no capture."
  area_scoring:
    black_stones_on_board: 7   # C1-C5, D4, A3
    black_territory: 9         # A3 no longer empty
    black_area_score: 16       # unchanged from R9: a territory point became a stone point
    white_area_score: 16       # unchanged
    white_final_with_komi: 23.5
    margin: "White by 7.5 — same as R9; filling one's own territory is free under area scoring."
  territory_scoring:
    black_territory: 9         # down by 1, nothing gained back
    black_prisoners: 0
    black_territory_score: 9
    white_territory_score: 10
    white_final_with_komi: 16.5
    margin: "White by 7.5 — up from 6.5 in R10; filling one's own territory cost Black a full point under territory scoring."
  significance: >
    This is the mechanism Ending the Game describes: the same extra move
    is free under area scoring and costs exactly one point under territory
    scoring, which is the usual cause of the two methods' margins
    diverging by more than their standard-komi offset.
```

## R12 — two passes end the main phase

```
    A B C
  1 . X .
  2 . O .
```

Any position; shown here as a minimal example. Black passes. White passes (the second pass, immediately following Black's).

```
expected:
  id: R12-two-passes-end-play
  after_black_pass: main phase still open (one pass does not end play)
  after_white_pass: main phase ends; dead-stones settlement begins
  if_disagreement_during_settlement: >
    Play conventionally resumes from this point to resolve the disputed
    group by actual capture, per pass.md and dead-stones.md.
```

## R13 — handicap placement: fixed star points (9×9)

```
       A B C D E F G H J
    1  . . . . . . . . .
    2  . . . . . . . . .
    3  . . X . . . X . .
    4  . . . . . . . . .
    5  . . . . . . . . .
    6  . . . . . . . . .
    7  . . X . . . X . .
    8  . . . . . . . . .
    9  . . . . . . . . .
```

9×9 board (column `I` conventionally skipped in Go coordinate letters, hence `A`–`H`, `J`). A 4-stone handicap, placed on the four corner star points: `C3`, `G3`, `C7`, `G7`.

```
expected:
  id: R13-handicap-fixed-star-points
  handicap_stones: 4
  points: [C3, G3, C7, G7]
  agreement: >
    All five rulesets in rulesets.md set
    ruleset.<name>.handicap_placement = fixed_star_points, and place a
    4-stone handicap at exactly these four points on a 9x9 board (the
    center point, E5, is the fifth star point, used starting at a 5-stone
    handicap but left empty here).
```

## What comes next

Return to [Rulesets](./rulesets.md) for the parameter definitions these positions exercise, or [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md) for the procedural narrative around R7 through R12. R2 and R3 are flagged above as structural specifications rather than fully traced sequences — implementers should construct and verify an exact move list against the kernel's own board-history representation before trusting them as literal test fixtures; every other position in this appendix (R1, R4 through R13) was hand-verified point by point during authoring.

rooms.title: Rulesets
rooms.description: Audience: kernel implementers and readers who already understand ko, suicide, seki, and both scoring methods. A comparison of five rulesets across five parameters, with a stable identifier for each cell so this document can be encoded directly as the kernel's ruleset data.
rooms.body:
Audience: kernel implementers and readers who already understand [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md), [suicide](../../../glossary/terms/suicide.md), [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md), and both scoring methods, per [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md).

Learning goal: fix, for five widely-played rulesets, the exact value of the five parameters that most affect play — ko regime, suicide, scoring method, standard komi, and handicap placement — precisely enough that each cell below is a rule object, not prose. Per the [Weiqi Platform Plan](./weiqi-platform-plan.md), this document *is* the kernel's ruleset spec: `@lenticule-science/weiqi-kernel` should be able to encode `ruleset.<name>.<parameter>` directly from the identifiers used here, as declared rule objects rather than code forks.

See also: [Weiqi Rulesets](./weiqi-rulesets.md) is this specification's learner-facing companion, explaining the same five rulesets in prose for readers comparing a club, server, or tournament rather than implementing a kernel.

## Comparison table

| Ruleset | Ko regime | Suicide | Scoring | Standard komi (even game) | Handicap placement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chinese | Positional superko | Illegal | Area | 7.5 | Fixed star points |
| Japanese | Simple ko only | Illegal | Territory | 6.5 | Fixed star points |
| AGA | Situational superko | Illegal | Area or territory (reconciled by pass stone) | 7.5 (area) / 6.5 (territory) | Fixed star points |
| New Zealand | Positional superko | Legal (any size) | Area | 7 | Fixed star points |
| Ing | Positional superko | Illegal | Area | 8 | Fixed star points |

## Stable identifiers

Each cell above is addressable as `ruleset.<name>.<parameter>`, matching the [ontology](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md)'s intent that the engine be the executable form of the glossary. The five ruleset names are `chinese`, `japanese`, `aga`, `newzealand`, `ing`. The five parameter names, and the value vocabulary each one draws from, are:

```
ko_regime          : simple_ko | positional_superko | situational_superko
suicide             : illegal | legal
scoring             : area | territory | area_or_territory
komi                : <number> (points added to White's score in an even game)
handicap_placement  : fixed_star_points | free_placement
```

```
ruleset.chinese.ko_regime         = positional_superko
ruleset.chinese.suicide           = illegal
ruleset.chinese.scoring           = area
ruleset.chinese.komi              = 7.5
ruleset.chinese.handicap_placement = fixed_star_points

ruleset.japanese.ko_regime        = simple_ko
ruleset.japanese.suicide          = illegal
ruleset.japanese.scoring          = territory
ruleset.japanese.komi             = 6.5
ruleset.japanese.handicap_placement = fixed_star_points

ruleset.aga.ko_regime             = situational_superko
ruleset.aga.suicide               = illegal
ruleset.aga.scoring               = area_or_territory
ruleset.aga.komi                  = 7.5   # area count
ruleset.aga.komi_territory        = 6.5   # territory count, reconciled via the pass-stone rule
ruleset.aga.handicap_placement    = fixed_star_points

ruleset.newzealand.ko_regime      = positional_superko
ruleset.newzealand.suicide        = legal
ruleset.newzealand.scoring        = area
ruleset.newzealand.komi           = 7
ruleset.newzealand.handicap_placement = fixed_star_points

ruleset.ing.ko_regime             = positional_superko
ruleset.ing.suicide               = illegal
ruleset.ing.scoring               = area
ruleset.ing.komi                  = 8
ruleset.ing.handicap_placement    = fixed_star_points
```

## Notes per parameter

**Ko regime.** [Simple ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) forbids only the single immediate recapture; it is the shared baseline every ruleset here includes. [Superko](../../../glossary/terms/superko.md) extends that ban to any repeated whole-board position. Japanese rules are the outlier: they specify no formal superko rule at all, relying instead on the two-pass-and-agree convention for ordinary games and a "no result" (rematch) ruling for the rare unresolved long cycle such as triple ko [@nihonkiin1989rules]. AGA rules specify situational superko explicitly [@usgo2022agarules]; Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules are generally implemented with positional superko in modern digital play, though traditional over-the-board Chinese rules historically left long cycles to ad hoc agreement much like Japanese rules do [@britgo2025default]. A kernel targeting strict traditional Chinese play should treat `ruleset.chinese.ko_regime` as configurable rather than fixed.

**Suicide.** [New Zealand rules](../../../glossary/terms/suicide.md) are the standard citation for legal suicide of any size; every other ruleset in this table forbids it entirely [@nzgo2013rules].

**Scoring.** [Area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md) counts stones plus territory; [territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md) counts territory plus prisoners only. AGA rules are unusual in supporting both, reconciled so the two counts normally agree via the pass-stone convention described in [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) [@usgo2022agarules].

**Standard komi.** Values above are the modern standard for an even game with no handicap; historical values have differed (Japanese komi was commonly 5.5 before a widely-adopted 2002 shift to 6.5, and Chinese komi has likewise moved between 5.5, 7.5, and other values across the twentieth century) [@britannica2026go]. The roughly one-point gap between Chinese-style area komi (7.5) and Japanese territory komi (6.5) is not arbitrary: it approximates the systematic scoring difference explained in [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md#why-area-and-territory-rarely-differ), where area scoring credits Black with one extra stone that territory scoring does not. Ing komi (8) reflects a separately-set tradition rather than the same offset logic.

**Handicap placement.** All five rulesets here place handicap stones on the fixed star points (hoshi) standard for the board size, in the conventional 2-through-9-stone patterns; none of the five mandates free placement as a rule, though free placement is sometimes used informally in casual or teaching games under any ruleset.

## What comes next

Return to [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md) for the procedural context these parameters govern, or continue to the [regression positions appendix](./regression-positions.md), which exercises several of these parameters — ko regime, suicide, and both scoring methods — against small labeled board positions.

rooms.title: Seki and False Eyes
rooms.description: Audience: readers who already understand eyes, connection, and life and death and want to work through positions where the ordinary two-eyes rule does not directly apply.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who already understand eyes, connection, and life and death and want to work through positions where the ordinary two-eyes rule does not directly apply.

Learning goal: recognize a seki when neither side can safely fill a shared liberty, and recognize a false eye when an eye-shaped point does not actually protect a group.

## Worked example: two groups sharing two liberties

Imagine a small region near the side of the board where a Black group and a White group are packed against each other and against the edge. Both groups are otherwise completely enclosed, connected to nothing else alive elsewhere on the board, and neither has an [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md) of its own. Between the two groups sit exactly two empty points, side by side, and those two points are the only [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md) either group has left.

Neither player can safely act on those two points. If Black plays on one of them, Black fills one of Black's own group's last two liberties, along with one of White's, and Black's group drops to a single liberty: [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md). White then plays the remaining shared point and captures the entire Black group. The same logic runs in reverse if White moves first: White's group ends up in atari, and Black captures. Because moving first into the shared space is always worse than leaving it alone, neither player ever plays there, and the position holds for the rest of the game. This is [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md): both groups stay on the board, alive, without either one ever forming two separate eyes.

Scoring this position depends on the ruleset. Under Japanese territory scoring, the two shared points earn nobody any points, because they were never enclosed as one player's exclusive territory [@britgo2026compare]. Under Chinese-style area scoring, each side's living stones count toward its score along with whatever territory it alone encloses elsewhere, but the two shared points still belong to neither side, since area scoring counts stones and exclusively-enclosed empty points, not disputed ones [@britgo2026compare]. The stones survive under either ruleset; only the point total for that local exchange differs.

## Worked example: an eye that is not really an eye

Now imagine a Black group that has enclosed a single empty point in what looks like a normal eye: the point itself is empty, and every intersection directly orthogonal to it is a Black stone. This point sits on the first line, directly along the side of the board (not in a corner). But of the diagonal points next to it, only one is Black, and that stone is a lone stone with few liberties of its own and no solid [connection](../../../glossary/terms/connection.md) to the rest of the group. The other relevant diagonal belongs to White.

An eye's security depends on more than its four orthogonal neighbors. The defending color also needs to control enough of the diagonal points around it: one diagonal if the eye sits in a corner, two if it sits on an edge, and three if it sits in the middle of the board [@senseislibrary2026falseeye]. This eye is on the edge, so Black needs two secure diagonals and has only one, and that one is itself capturable. If White captures the weak diagonal stone, White gets a stone directly next to the eye point. The point is then no longer surrounded solely by connected Black stones, so White can play into it. That makes this a [false eye](../../../glossary/terms/false-eye.md): a point that currently looks like a second eye but can eventually be forced open.

If this is the only other candidate eye the group has besides one genuine eye elsewhere, the group does not have two real eyes yet. Under ordinary [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md) reading, one true eye plus one false eye counts as one eye, not two, and a group with only one secure eye is not unconditionally alive. It survives only if it can still make a second true eye somewhere else, or if the surrounding position turns into a capturing race or a seki instead.

## Exercises

1. In the two-group seki above, why does playing at either shared point immediately backfire on the player who plays it?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Filling one shared liberty removes one of the mover's own last two liberties, dropping that group into atari with only the other shared point left. The opponent's group still has that same point as its own last liberty, so the opponent plays it and captures. Because the same backfire happens to whichever side moves first, both sides prefer to leave the two points alone indefinitely.
</details>

2. Why can a single weakly connected diagonal stone turn a real-looking eye into a false eye?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

An eye on the edge is secure only if the defending color holds at least two of the diagonal points around it, not just the four orthogonal points. If one of those diagonals depends on a stone that can itself be captured, the opponent can remove that stone and gain a stone directly next to the eye point, which breaks the enclosure that made the point a protected liberty in the first place.
</details>

## What comes next

Seki and false eyes are both exceptions to the simple version of "two eyes live" introduced in [Living Groups and Eyes](./living-groups-and-eyes.md), so it is worth rereading that lesson's eye-shape discussion once these two ideas are clear. For the scoring consequences of seki under different rulesets, continue with [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md). For vocabulary work, continue with [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md), especially [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md), [false eye](../../../glossary/terms/false-eye.md), [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md), and [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md).

rooms.title: History of Weiqi
rooms.body:
Weiqi's history is a long record of transmission and institutional refinement: a game that began in China, spread across East Asia, and later became a global competitive and educational tradition.

## Worked example: one game, three names

The same game is commonly called *weiqi* in Chinese, *baduk* in Korean, and *go* in Japanese-derived English usage [@britannica2026go; @igf2026historyofgo]. Those names mark more than translation. They show the route by which the game moved across linguistic and institutional settings while keeping a recognizable rules core.

## Origins in China

The game originated in China more than two millennia ago, and some accounts place it much earlier [@britannica2026go; @igf2026historyofgo]. Early Chinese traditions treated it not only as recreation but as a cultivated art associated with scholarly accomplishment.

What matters historically is durability. Weiqi kept the same basic logic of placement, enclosure, and capture across centuries even as rule explanations, board conventions, and social settings changed.

## Transmission across East Asia

Weiqi spread from China to Korea and Japan, where it developed strong local traditions and institutions [@igf2026historyofgo]. Japanese professional houses later played a major role in codifying teaching lineages, recording famous games, and circulating the name *go* beyond Japan.

This transmission changed how the game was taught and organized, but not its basic identity. The core mechanics remained territorial placement, [capture](../../../glossary/terms/capture.md), and shape judgment. The major historical shifts were institutional and cultural rather than mechanical.

## Modern international play

In the twentieth century, weiqi expanded far beyond East Asia through national associations, translated teaching materials, and international federations [@igf2026historyofgo; @britgo2026whatisgo]. That growth made rank systems, tournament rules, and teaching methods more legible to new players outside the game's older centers.

One important feature of that modern spread is accessibility across skill levels. Organizations outside East Asia often present [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) play as a normal and valuable part of the game, not as a lesser version of it [@britgo2026whatisgo]. That emphasis helped weiqi travel as both a competitive discipline and a teachable social practice.

## Exercises

1. What does the existence of the names *weiqi*, *baduk*, and *go* show about the game's history?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

It shows that the game spread across different linguistic and institutional settings while preserving a recognizable core structure.
</details>

2. What changed most as weiqi spread internationally: its basic mechanics or its institutions of teaching and competition?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Its institutions changed more than its basic mechanics. The game kept the same territorial placement logic while different regions developed their own teaching systems, organizations, and naming traditions.
</details>

## What comes next

The next useful move is to return from chronology to structure through [Living Groups and Eyes](./living-groups-and-eyes.md), then follow the rule-balancing side of the game in [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md). The local [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md) define the recurring tactical vocabulary directly.

# Weiqi Kernel Constitution

Audience: the 561 Group board and agents that will materialize, extend, or consume `weiqi-kernel`.

Learning goal: know exactly what `weiqi-kernel` is for, what it may and must refuse, who owns it, and on what authority it exists — before any of its filesystem projections are treated as settled.

## Governance basis

This record was produced without the reference its assigning instruction named: `.agents/skills/corpus-normalization/references/service-section-constitution.md` does not exist anywhere in this repository (confirmed by direct read attempt and repository-wide search). No prior constitution record of any kind exists yet to serve as a working exemplar either — this is the first. In the absence of both, this record is built from the next-best evidence, in the order `references/repository-model.md` itself prescribes (explicit instruction, then authoritative content inside the payload, then local form, then generic convention):

- the [Weiqi Platform Plan](./weiqi-platform-plan.md), §"Governance and placement" and §"Board decisions requested" (board-approved 2026-08-18) — the direct authorizing text and field list (purpose, inputs/outputs, customers, boundary, refusal conditions);
- the board's own 2026-08-18 note, "Board challenge: constituting service sections" (`561-group-board-of-directors-leader-assistant-services-section`) — the four-face admission/constitution/materialization/conformance split, and the acceptance test that a constitution record must be complete and reviewable *before* the filesystem is touched;
- the board's 2026-08-11 derivation, "The standard form of packages and sections, derived from the mathematics" — the definitions this record uses for *service* (a fiber with an addressable apex; the package manifest is one projection of that apex, not its identity), *generative parent* (containment must match generation — a section contains a service only if the service is generated from the section's apex), and *closed-world signature* (a service's reach is exactly its declared operators, nothing borrowed).

This record's disposition: `weiqi-services-section` is asked by the plan to gain a `services/` child named `weiqi-kernel`. The plan itself also states "no speculative scaffolding — each child directory appears only when its first real artifact does." A constitution record is not the kernel's first real artifact; it is the parent section's own act of admission. This document therefore lives in the parent's `content/`, not inside a newly fabricated `services/weiqi-kernel/` directory, so that admission does not itself become the scaffolding the plan forbids.

## Distinct responsibility

Legal-move determination, ko/superko regimes, ruleset parameterization, area/territory scoring with seki and dead-stone protocol, SGF parse/serialize, and the semantic event layer that recognizes glossary concepts in move sequences are one indivisible responsibility: producing and annotating legal weiqi positions with no dependency on a network, a clock it was not handed, or a rendering surface. No existing service in this repository owns "correct, glossary-linked weiqi rules as pure computation" — `weiqi-services-section` currently owns only corpus content (lessons, glossary, rulesets-as-prose), not executable rules. Absorbing this responsibility into the content tree would make prose and code indistinguishable in ownership terms; absorbing it into a future play service would tie a pure, browser-and-Node-portable computation to a stateful, keyed, socketed process that the purity spine (2026-08-11 derivation, §5) explicitly forbids mixing. A distinct owner is therefore required, and none exists.

## Generative parent

`weiqi-services-section` (`lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/science-services-section/services/agent-services-section/services/play-services-section/services/game-science-services-section/services/board-games-services-section/services/weiqi-services-section/`).

The 2026-08-11 derivation's Clause 3.3 requires containment to match generation: a section contains a service only if the service is generated from the section's apex. `weiqi-kernel` is generated directly from the corpus this section already owns — the plan states the build motto outright: "the engine is the executable form of the glossary. Each glossary term corresponds to a named predicate or event in the rules kernel." The kernel's semantic event layer is a direct, named transform of `weiqi-services-section`'s own seventeen glossary terms and its rulesets/regression-positions references (`content/text/documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md`, `regression-positions.md`). No other section generates it.

## Form: a singular service, not a services-section

The 2026-08-11 derivation gives the test directly (echoed by the board's 2026-08-18 challenge note): if a candidate's faces have distinct inputs, outputs, and refusal conditions, they form a covered section; if they collapse to one inseparable operation, the correct form is a singular service.

Applying it: position representation, legal-move determination, ko/superko regimes, scoring, SGF parse/serialize, and the semantic event layer share one input type (a position plus a move or move sequence, under one ruleset), one output type (a new position, a legality verdict, a score, or an annotated event stream), one test suite (round-trip SGF, ko/superko invariants, scoring cross-checks against the corpus's own regression positions), one manifest, and one customer relationship (anything that needs correct rules, embedded as a library, not addressed over a network). They do not glue into a nontrivial cover with overlaps and restriction maps between sub-services — declaring them as separate covered services would only produce Clause 2.2's degenerate case (zero-disagreement overlaps, vacuously coherent) dressed up as structure. `weiqi-kernel` is therefore constituted as a **singular service**, not a `weiqi-kernel-services-section`.

**Open naming tension, not resolved here.** The plan calls the working npm name `@lenticule-science/weiqi-kernel` "subject to the constitution step," and this repository's own convention for a singular leaf service under a `services/` container is near-universally a `-service`-suffixed name (`solitaire-service`, `climate-research-service`, `json-codec-service`, and dozens more; zero unsuffixed counterexamples found under any `services/` directory). Separately, the same 2026-08-11 derivation's Clause 5 product spine reserves `apps/<domain>-computer` for exactly this kernel's shape — "operational but pure: no network, no keys, no clock it was not handed" — with `services/<domain>-server` reserved for where keys and sockets actually enter, which this kernel never does. This record does not resolve either tension by fiat, in keeping with the house rule that collisions are represented and either glue uniquely or produce a quantified refusal rather than being settled by a convenient winner. Both are carried forward as open obligations below, for the materialization step's explicit authority to settle rather than for this constitution to presume.

## Purpose

Compute and annotate legal weiqi play as a pure function of declared rules: given a position, a ruleset, and a move or move sequence, determine legality, apply captures, detect and enforce the ruleset's ko/superko regime, score a finished or scoring-request position (area or territory, with seki and dead-stone resolution), and recognize the glossary's semantic events (atari, capture, ko started/resolved, group connected/cut, eye formed/falsified, group settled/killed) as they occur. Parse and serialize positions and game records as SGF. Nothing in this purpose ever writes to a network, a database, or a clock the caller did not hand it.

## Inputs

- A position (immutable representation) and, where relevant, its history (for ko/superko).
- A ruleset, supplied as a declared data object (Chinese, Japanese, AGA, New Zealand, Ing — rules as data, never as code forks), including the superko regime and komi/handicap parameters.
- A move, or an SGF-encoded move sequence / game record, to apply, validate, or annotate.
- A scoring or dead-stone-marking request against a position under a chosen ruleset.

## Outputs

- A legality verdict for a proposed move, or the resulting position after a legal move (captures applied).
- Ko/superko state needed to judge the next move.
- A score (area or territory) with seki resolved and dead stones settled, under the requested ruleset.
- Serialized SGF for any position or game record; a parsed position/game record from SGF input.
- A semantic event stream: named events corresponding one-to-one with glossary terms this section already defines, each event carrying enough position data for a caller to render or narrate it.
- Zobrist hashes sufficient for superko detection and position-identity comparisons.

## Customers

Any component that needs authoritative, glossary-linked weiqi rules and does not itself want to implement them: the platform's static Learn app (board component, interactive lessons, tsumego player) and, later, the Durable-Object play service (`weiqi-platform`'s future play face) as its sole source of move validation, scoring, and event annotation. The kernel has no customer relationship with end users directly — it is a library dependency, never a network-addressed endpoint.

## Authority

- **Closed-world signature (2026-08-11 derivation, Clause 3.2):** the kernel may be invoked only through its declared constructors and operators — position construction, move application, scoring, SGF parse/serialize, and event annotation. No caller may reach into kernel internals to bypass ko/superko or scoring logic; there is no other door.
- **Stratum:** L2 (games/strategies), per the ontological-spine tower cited in the 2026-08-11 derivation — the kernel encodes a game's rule structure, one level above L1 agency and below L3 computing/services. It must not import from any L3 package (nothing that opens a socket, a database handle, or a clock).
- **Change authority:** changes to rules-of-the-game content (which ruleset variants exist, which events the semantic layer recognizes) are downstream of `weiqi-services-section`'s own corpus — a new glossary term or rulesets-reference entry is upstream evidence for a kernel change, not the reverse. The kernel does not originate rules content; it executes what the corpus already defines, per the plan's stated motto.
- **Runtime authority:** none beyond what any pure library has. It holds no credentials, no persistent state, and no independent authority to act — it only computes when called.

## Non-ownership

`weiqi-kernel` does not own: corpus content (lessons, glossary terms, rulesets-as-prose — these remain `weiqi-services-section`'s own `content/`); rendering or UI (the board component, hover-cards, lesson interactivity belong to `weiqi-platform`); persistence, accounts, ratings, or matchmaking (D1/Durable-Object concerns belong to the future play service); bots or engine analysis (GnuGo/KataGo integration is explicitly platform/operations territory in the plan, not kernel territory); and network or transport of any kind. It does not own naming its own final package identity or directory suffix — see "Open naming tension" above, deferred to materialization.

## Refusal conditions

The kernel must refuse (return an explicit error/verdict, never a silent best-effort guess) when:

- a proposed move is illegal under the supplied ruleset (occupied point, suicide where the ruleset forbids it, ko/superko violation under the declared regime);
- a ruleset object is malformed or does not declare a required parameter (superko regime, komi, handicap points) the requested operation needs;
- a scoring request is made against a position that is not settled and no dead-stone marking has been supplied where the ruleset requires one;
- SGF input does not parse as well-formed SGF, or round-trips to a different position than it encoded;
- an operation is invoked outside the closed-world signature declared above (no internal escape hatch is provided for any caller, including the platform).

The kernel must never silently degrade a ruleset, guess a caller's intent on malformed input, or produce a position/score it cannot justify against its own declared rules.

## Board authorization

The 561 Group board approved the Weiqi Platform Plan (`content/text/documents/articles/notes/weiqi-platform-plan.md`, dated 2026-08-18) on 2026-08-18, including its "Board decisions requested" item 1: "Approve platform placement inside `weiqi-services-section` and the two child-section constitutions (kernel, platform app)." This record discharges that authorization's kernel half. It authorizes the *constitution* recorded here — the existence, boundary, and authority of `weiqi-kernel` as a service — and does not by itself authorize materialization of any filesystem, package, or protocol projection, per the board challenge note's acceptance test 4 ("refuse materialization without explicit authority"). Materialization is the next, separately-gated workflow step.

## Open obligations

- **Naming form**, stated above: `weiqi-kernel` (bare) vs. a `-service`-suffixed corpus-conventional name, and `services/weiqi-kernel` vs. an `apps/<domain>-computer`-tier placement under the 2026-08-11 derivation's purity spine. Both readings are defensible from the documents; neither is settled by this record.
- **Pre-existing uncommitted artifact at the wrong address.** At the time this record was written, `weiqi-services-section/apps/weiqi-kernel/` already contains real, uncommitted source (`game.mts`, `board.mts`, `scoring.mts`, `rulesets.mts`, `zobrist.mts`, `position.mts`, `events.mts`, a `test/` directory, and a `package.json` naming `@lenticule-science/weiqi-kernel`) — untracked in git, not reflected in this section's own `README.md` (which still reads "No engine, kernel, or app code exists yet"). This is exactly the inversion the board's 2026-08-18 challenge warns against: a real artifact materializing ahead of its constitution. This record does not move, rename, or otherwise touch that code — doing so is materialization, out of this record's scope — but flags it as the first thing the materialization step must reconcile against whichever address the open naming question above settles on.
- **Restricted-Yoneda leg agreement** (2026-08-11 derivation, Clause 1.2/PPA-FR-040) remains an open obligation of the corpus generally: this record's identification of `weiqi-kernel`'s "apex" with its eventual npm manifest, protocol shape, and conformance vector is a checked runtime condition once those legs exist, not an assumed fact now.
- **2026-08-19 materialization decision.** The naming-form obligation above is now resolved: the kernel is materialized at `apps/weiqi-kernel` (bare name, no `-service` suffix), not under `services/`. This follows directly from the board's 2026-08-11 product-spine derivation, Clause 5: pure, no-network packages belong at the `apps/<domain>-computer` purity tier, and `weiqi-kernel` — no socket, no key, no clock it was not handed — is exactly that shape, not the `services/<domain>-server` tier reserved for where keys and sockets actually enter. This also reconciles the pre-existing-artifact obligation above: `apps/weiqi-kernel` is the settled address the code already occupied, not a second candidate awaiting reconciliation. The kernel's test suite state (pass/fail counts and how to run them) is recorded in the kernel's own README (`apps/weiqi-kernel/README.md`), not duplicated here.

## What comes next

Once the board or its delegate settles the naming-form open obligation, the materialization step may translate this constitution into package, filesystem, and (where the naming lands on `apps/`) conformance projections — reconciling the pre-existing `apps/weiqi-kernel/` code against whichever address is chosen, rather than leaving two candidate homes for one apex. See the sibling [Weiqi Platform Constitution](./weiqi-platform-constitution.md) for the child that consumes this kernel.

rooms.body:
# Weiqi Learn Constitution

Audience: the 561 Group board and agents that will materialize, extend, or consume `weiqi-platform-learn-service`.

Learning goal: know exactly what the Learn service is for, what it may and must refuse, who owns it, and on what authority it exists — before any of its filesystem projections are treated as settled.

## Governance basis

This record uses the same governance basis as its siblings [Weiqi Kernel Constitution](./weiqi-kernel-constitution.md) and [Weiqi Platform Constitution](./weiqi-platform-constitution.md), repeated rather than assumed: `.agents/skills/corpus-normalization/references/service-section-constitution.md` still does not exist anywhere in this repository. This record instead draws on `references/repository-model.md`'s evidence order, the board-approved [Weiqi Platform Plan](./weiqi-platform-plan.md), the board's 2026-08-18 "Board challenge: constituting service sections" note, and the board's 2026-08-11 "standard form" derivation — and, directly, on the [Weiqi Platform Constitution](./weiqi-platform-constitution.md) itself, which named this exact record as an owed act in its "Open obligations": "The Learn service's own constitution record is still owed. This document constitutes the section; it is not a substitute for `weiqi-platform-learn-service`'s own record (purpose/inputs/outputs/customers/authority/non-ownership/refusal conditions at the service level, generative parent = this section). That record — and only after it exists — is what licenses a `services/weiqi-platform/…` (or `apps/…`) directory to appear for the Learn face." This record is that owed act, and its existence is precisely what licenses the materialization decision recorded below.

## Distinct responsibility

Rendering weiqi instruction — a board, interactive lessons, a tsumego player, glossary hover-cards, and a learner's local progress against the concept graph — entirely client-side, with no account and no server round-trip, is a responsibility no existing service owns. `weiqi-kernel` computes rules but must stay pure (no rendering); `weiqi-services-section`'s `content/` holds prose but is not an interactive surface; the sibling Play face (declared, not admitted) is the mirror-image responsibility — authenticated, stateful, keyed and socketed — that the platform constitution's own purity boundary forbids mixing into this one. The platform constitution's Clause-2 cover test already decided the two faces are distinct (§"Form: a services-section, not a singular service"); this record constitutes the Learn half of that decided cover as its own service, on the same grounds the kernel used to constitute itself relative to the section that generates it.

## Generative parent

`weiqi-platform-services-section` (`lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/science-services-section/services/agent-services-section/services/play-services-section/services/game-science-services-section/services/board-games-services-section/services/weiqi-services-section/services/weiqi-platform/`, per the materialization decision below).

The 2026-08-11 derivation's Clause 3.3 requires containment to match generation. The platform constitution names the Learn service as the first member of its own declared cover (§"Cover, overlaps, and stratum") and states outright that this section, not `weiqi-services-section` directly, is what "admits" it. Containment therefore runs: `weiqi-services-section` generates `weiqi-platform-services-section` (per that constitution's own "Generative parent"), which in turn generates `weiqi-platform-learn-service` as a declared cover member. No other section generates it, and this record does not re-derive what the platform constitution already settled about the section's own generative parent — it only extends the chain one level.

## Form: a singular service, not a services-section

Applying the same test the kernel and platform constitutions both use: does the candidate decompose into faces with distinct inputs, outputs, and refusal conditions, or does it collapse to one inseparable operation?

The Learn service's own components — board rendering, tutorial flow, tsumego checking, glossary lookup, hover-cards, lesson playback — share one input type (a learner's local navigation/selection plus the kernel's pure computation), one output type (rendered instructional DOM state, held in the browser, never persisted past the session), one test posture (`node:test` over pure logic modules, DOM kept out of module top-level per the house rule), one manifest, one deploy artifact (static assets, "deployable exactly like 561.group," per the plan), and one customer relationship (an anonymous learner, directly; the kernel and the section's corpus, as read-only dependencies). None of these sub-components has a refusal condition distinct from the whole service's own — none independently holds a key, a socket, or a persistent write path, and none is separately gated by the board. This does not glue into a nontrivial cover with overlaps and restriction maps; it is Clause 1.1's single fiber. `weiqi-platform-learn-service` is therefore constituted as a **singular service**, not a `weiqi-platform-learn-services-section` — matching the kernel's own form-finding, not the platform's.

## Purpose

Teach weiqi interactively, entirely client-side, over one shared concept graph: render a board, step a learner through the corpus's lesson template as interactive worked examples, run a graded tsumego player with revealed commentary on request, and surface glossary hover-cards at the moment the kernel's own semantic events make a term relevant — the platform's stated differentiator, applied to its first admitted face. Ships complete and usable on its own, per the plan's education-first sequencing, before any multiplayer complexity is admitted.

## Inputs

- A learner's navigation and selection: which lesson, which tsumego problem, which glossary term, which move to attempt on the board.
- The kernel's pure computation: legality verdicts, resulting positions, scoring, SGF, and the semantic event stream (`weiqi-kernel`, consumed read-only, never reimplemented).
- This section's own corpus content: the lesson template, the seventeen glossary terms, the ontology (rendered as a skill tree), and tsumego problem data — authored in `content/`, consumed here only as rendered data, per the platform constitution's non-ownership clause.
- No account, no server round-trip, no data the render call was not directly handed.

## Outputs

- Rendered board state (SVG board component, themeable, faithful at 9/13/19 with star points, last-move and annotation layers).
- Step-through interactive lessons converted from the corpus's lesson template, including the capture-go ladder tutorial.
- A playable, graded tsumego player with commentary revealed on request.
- Glossary hover-cards, attached wherever rendered content carries a `termRef` back to this section's own corpus.
- A learner's local progress against the concept graph, held client-side only — never a server-persisted record (that is Play-face territory, not admitted).

## Customers

An anonymous or lightly-identified learner needing no account — the plan's explicit Phase 1 target, "no account required" for the first session. Internally, this service is a customer of `weiqi-kernel` (rules, scoring, events) and of `weiqi-services-section`'s own corpus content (lessons, glossary, ontology); it produces no rules content and no corpus content of its own, per the platform constitution's non-ownership clause, which this record inherits rather than restates in full.

## Authority

- **Closed-world signature:** this service may only invoke the kernel's declared public API (`Game`, `getRuleset`, `scoreArea`/`scoreTerritory`, SGF, semantic events with `termRef`, `findGroup`, `boardHash`) and its own declared modules. It holds no network operator, no key operator, no socket operator at all — the purity boundary the platform constitution assigns to the Learn face (§"Authority") is this service's entire declared signature, not a subset of a larger one.
- **Change authority:** UI, interaction, and lesson-rendering decisions are this service's own; rules decisions are never this service's to make. Any disagreement between what this service renders and what the kernel computes is resolved in the kernel's favor, always — per the kernel's own constitution and the platform constitution's restriction on the declared kernel/board/hover-card overlap, which this service must restrict to identically rather than diverge from.
- **Runtime authority:** none beyond what any static client-side asset has. No credentials, no persistent state, no independent authority to act.
- **Non-mutating preview is this service's own to provide.** The kernel's `Game.isLegal(move)` returns a boolean only and offers no non-mutating preview and no capture-go ruleset (per the kernel's public API as constituted); this service's `kernel-bridge` layer supplies both by replaying a scratch `Game` and by layering a capture-go win condition over the kernel's existing ruleset/event vocabulary, never by adding new rules logic the kernel itself should own. This is application-layer convenience over the kernel's declared operators, not a new rules capability — the closed-world signature above still holds.

## Non-ownership

`weiqi-platform-learn-service` does not own: rules logic of any kind (legality, scoring, ko/superko, SGF, semantic-event recognition — all `weiqi-kernel`'s, consumed read-only); corpus authorship (lessons, glossary terms, tsumego problems, ontology remain `weiqi-services-section`'s own `content/`, authored there, rendered here); the Play face's responsibilities (accounts, live sockets, authoritative game rooms, persisted game/rating records — declared but not admitted, and in any case never this service's to build); bot/engine hosting (GnuGo, KataGo, the bare-metal analysis box are explicitly out of the platform's boundary per the plan); and billing/monetization (out of scope per the plan and the platform constitution alike).

## Refusal conditions

- This service must refuse to open a network connection, hold a key, or read a clock it was not handed by its own render call — any such apparent need is evidence the responsibility belongs to the Play face, never a reason to compromise this service's purity, per the platform constitution's own refusal condition for the Learn face, inherited here at the service level.
- This service must refuse to reimplement or shadow kernel logic (legality, scoring, event recognition) locally "for speed" or convenience; any move validation not delegated to `weiqi-kernel` is a refusal-worthy violation of the platform's declared overlap restriction. Its own capture-go win condition and non-mutating preview (see Authority, above) are the one licensed exception, and only insofar as they compose the kernel's existing declared operators rather than adding new ones.
- This service must refuse to persist a learner's progress, or any other state, past the browser session in any server-reachable location — it has no persistent write path, structurally, per its closed-world signature.
- This service must refuse to let its board-rendering or glossary/event-naming logic diverge from whatever the Play face eventually adopts, per the platform's declared restriction; a detected divergence is a defect in the section's health, not local team preference.

## Board authorization

The 561 Group board approved the Weiqi Platform Plan (`content/text/documents/articles/notes/weiqi-platform-plan.md`, dated 2026-08-18) on 2026-08-18, including its "Board decisions requested" item 1 ("Approve platform placement inside `weiqi-services-section` and the two child-section constitutions (kernel, platform app)") and item 5 ("Confirm education-first sequencing (Phase 1 ships before any multiplayer)"). The [Weiqi Platform Constitution](./weiqi-platform-constitution.md) discharged that authorization's section-level half and explicitly named this Learn-service record as the next owed act, gating any `services/weiqi-platform/…` or `apps/…` directory on its existence (§"Open obligations", §"What comes next"). This record discharges that owed act. It authorizes the *constitution* of `weiqi-platform-learn-service` and, per the same platform-constitution clause, now licenses the materialization decision recorded below — it does not separately re-authorize the Play face, which remains withheld per the platform constitution's own refusal condition until Phase 2 is separately authorized.

## Materialization decision (2026-08-19)

With this record written, the platform constitution's licensing condition is satisfied ("only after it exists" — see Governance basis, above), and materialization proceeds on the same product-spine grounds the kernel's own materialization decision used (2026-08-11 derivation, Clause 5):

- **The section materializes at `services/weiqi-platform/`**, not `apps/weiqi-platform/`, because — unlike the kernel — `weiqi-platform-services-section` is a *covered section* whose declared cover includes a future Play face that, once admitted, will hold keys, sockets, and a clock (per the platform constitution's own §"Form" and §"Stratum": the Play face "sits at the `services/<domain>-server` sub-tier"). A section that covers a future keyed/socketed member is not the pure-package shape Clause 5 reserves for `apps/`; it belongs at the `services/` tier the section as a whole will eventually justify, even though only its pure member is admitted today. The section's own filesystem projection carries a `README.md` and `package.json` per house form, named `@lenticule-science/weiqi-platform-services-section`, declaring its cover (`weiqi-platform-learn-service` admitted; `weiqi-platform-play-service` declared, not admitted) exactly as the platform constitution states it — the manifest is a projection of the already-decided cover, not a second place to redecide it.
- **The Learn service materializes at `services/weiqi-platform/apps/weiqi-learn/`**, under the section's own `apps/` — not `services/` — subdirectory, because this record's own §"Form" and §"Authority" establish that the Learn service is exactly the pure, no-network, no-key, no-clock-it-was-not-handed shape Clause 5 reserves for `apps/<domain>-computer`, identically to how the kernel's own materialization decision placed `weiqi-kernel` at `apps/weiqi-kernel` rather than `services/weiqi-kernel`. The board's product-spine rule is a rule about a package's own purity, not about which container happens to hold it — a pure package sits at an `apps/` tier even when its immediate parent is a `services/`-tier section, because the section's tier reflects what its *cover as a whole* will eventually require, while the package's tier reflects what *it itself* requires now. Package name: `@lenticule-science/weiqi-learn`, plain browser-ready ESM (`.mjs`), no TypeScript, no framework, no dependency, no build step for its own code — only the one-time kernel-stripping build pipeline that copies the kernel's `.mts` sources to `public/lib/kernel/*.mjs` via `node:module`'s native type-stripping, per Node 24's stable support for it.
- This decision does not admit the Play face. Its cover entry in the section manifest remains declared, not materialized, per the platform constitution's own refusal condition ("must refuse to admit the Play face into its cover until Phase 1 has shipped and the board has separately authorized Phase 2").

## Open obligations

- **Naming form**, inherited unresolved from the platform constitution: `weiqi-platform` vs. `weiqi-platform-services-section` at the section level remains open there; this record's own service-level name, `weiqi-platform-learn-service` (doctrine) materializing as `@lenticule-science/weiqi-learn` (package), follows the kernel's own bare-name precedent for a pure `apps/`-tier package and is treated as settled by this record's own materialization decision above, not left open.
- **Restricted-Yoneda leg agreement** (2026-08-11 derivation, Clause 1.2/PPA-FR-040) applies here as it does to the kernel and the platform section: this service's identification of its own apex, manifest, and protocol legs is a checked runtime condition once those legs exist, not an assumed fact now.
- **Conformance against the platform's declared overlap** (kernel dependency, board component, hover-card component) is not computed by this record — per the platform constitution's §"Authority", that computation happens "once both members are admitted and materialized," and only the Learn member is admitted today. This record's own restriction (Authority and Refusal conditions, above) states the obligation; it does not discharge the check.

## What comes next

Code, README, and `package.json` may now appear under `services/weiqi-platform/` and `services/weiqi-platform/apps/weiqi-learn/`, per the materialization decision above — this record is the act that licenses them. See the sibling [Weiqi Kernel Constitution](./weiqi-kernel-constitution.md) for the service this app depends on and must never reimplement, and the [Weiqi Platform Constitution](./weiqi-platform-constitution.md) for the section this service is one declared member of.

# Weiqi LSP Authorization Record

The [weiqi-lsp constitution](weiqi-lsp-constitution.md) authorizes only `SPEC.md` and lists
ratification of weiqi-lsp as a third child service as an open obligation, directing that no
`src/`, `test/`, or `package.json` appear without explicit authority. On 2026-08-19 an
implementation pass correctly **refused** to materialize the service on those grounds
(the constitution's own acceptance test 4, honored in practice).

The explicit authority exists. The owner, 2026-08-19, to the session ringleader, verbatim:

> "Another agent was working on a weiqi-cli and it also got interrupted by our outage,
> restart it as part of our doing of weiqi stuff."

This record memorializes that directive as the authorization to materialize
`apps/weiqi-lsp` per its ratified-by-this-record `SPEC.md`. Scope and conditions:

1. Implementation follows `SPEC.md` as written; deviations carry stated reasons.
2. `apps/weiqi-kernel` remains read-only. The known SPEC gap (WQ005 references
   `COLUMN_LETTERS`, which the kernel does not export) is resolved by deriving the column
   alphabet through the kernel's exported `pointToCoord` — never by editing the kernel.
3. The kernel's 71/71 suite must pass untouched after materialization.

If the owner intends a different or narrower authorization, editing or deleting this
record withdraws it; the implementation would then be reverted on request.
