rooms.title: Weiqi Rulesets
rooms.description: Audience: readers who already understand territory, komi, and handicap and want to know which named ruleset governs a given club, server, or tournament, and why the differences rarely change who wins.
rooms.body:
Audience: readers who already understand [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md), [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md), and [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) and want to know which named ruleset governs a given club, server, or tournament, and why the differences rarely change who wins.

Learning goal: distinguish area scoring from territory scoring, compare standard komi and suicide legality across the Chinese, Japanese, AGA, New Zealand, and Ing rulesets, and explain why a beginner can safely postpone choosing among them.

See also: [Rulesets](./rulesets.md) is this lesson's implementer-facing companion, fixing the same five rulesets' ko-regime, suicide, scoring, komi, and handicap values as stable identifiers for the rules kernel rather than as club-facing prose.

## Worked example: one finished position, two ways of counting it

Picture a finished 9x9 game with no disputes left on the board. Black has a living group enclosing 12 empty points and has played 32 stones over the course of the game that remain on the board. White has a living group enclosing 15 empty points and has 31 stones remaining on the board. Nobody has left a seki, and every dead stone has already been removed by capture.

Counted under **territory rules**: Black's score is territory plus prisoners captured; White's score is territory plus prisoners captured, then White adds komi. Counted under **area rules**: Black's score is territory plus living stones on the board; White's score is territory plus living stones on the board, then White adds komi.

These are different arithmetic procedures, but they almost always produce the same winner by close to the same margin, because every point one player gains by playing an extra stone on the board (which only area scoring rewards directly) is a point the same player did not need to leave as territory (which both methods reward). The British Go Association's own comparison of rule sets puts it plainly: "the result of the two methods is usually the same to within one point" [@britgo2026compare]. That near-equivalence, not any deep philosophical difference between "area" and "territory" as goals, is the main thing to understand before looking at named rulesets.

## Area scoring vs. territory scoring

**Territory scoring** (used by Japanese and Korean rules) counts each player's surrounded empty points plus prisoners captured during the game, and does not otherwise count stones on the board [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Because stones themselves are worth nothing under this method, playing a stone inside your own [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md) without capturing anything turns a counted territory point into an uncounted stone, which is why filling in your own territory late in the game typically costs a point.

**Area scoring** (used by Chinese, AGA, New Zealand, and Ing rules) counts each player's surrounded empty points plus every living stone of that color remaining on the board [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Under area scoring, filling in your own territory does not cost anything, because the stone you added is worth exactly as much as the territory point it replaced. This is the practical difference that matters, not some difference in what counts as "winning."

## Why the two methods almost always agree

Across a full game, both players place roughly the same number of stones, including the neutral endgame points ([dame](../../../glossary/terms/dame.md)) that get filled in near the close of play. Area scoring pays a point for every stone on the board, including those dame-filling moves; territory scoring pays nothing for them. As long as both sides fill roughly equal numbers of dame points, that difference cancels out between the two players, leaving the margin between area and territory results at zero or one point [@britgo2026compare].

The two methods diverge in a few well-known situations rather than randomly:

- **[Seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md)** (a mutual standoff where neither side can profitably capture the other). Territory scoring gives no territory and no prisoners to either seki group, since nothing was captured and no space was ever "enclosed" territory. Area scoring still counts each living stone in the seki, so an uneven number of stones on each side of a seki can shift the count by a few points under area rules where it would not move at all under territory rules [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets].
- **Disputed dead stones.** Territory scoring requires the players to agree on which stones are dead before counting, because a stone left on the board uncounted is worth nothing either way. Area scoring lets a disagreement be settled by simply resuming play and capturing the stone, since filling in the extra move costs nothing. This is a procedural difference in how disputes get resolved, not a difference in the game's usual result.

These are corner cases. For an ordinary finished game with no seki and no disputed groups, area and territory scoring will hand the same player the win, usually by the same margin plus or minus a point tied to whichever side passed last.

## The named rulesets

### Japanese rules

Territory scoring; standard even-game komi is 6.5 points [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Suicide (playing a stone with no remaining [liberty](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md) that captures nothing) is forbidden. Only the simple [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) rule — no immediate one-move recapture that restores the prior position — is written into the rules; broader repeating whole-board positions have traditionally been ruled "no result," requiring the game to be replayed, rather than resolved by a general superko rule [@britgo2026compare].

### Korean rules

Territory scoring with the same 6.5 standard komi as Japanese rules, and the same general shape of rule set. Korean rules write out a more explicit procedure for repeated whole-board positions than Japanese rules do, but the outcome is the same: if neither player is willing to break the cycle, the game ends in a draw or "no result," not a decided winner [@gomagic2026rulesets].

### Chinese rules

Area scoring; standard even-game komi is 7.5 area points [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Suicide is forbidden. Chinese rules broadly forbid recreating any earlier whole-board position, which functions in practice like a positional superko rule, though the traditional rule text states it more simply than the AGA's formal version [@britgo2026compare; @gokgs2026rulesets].

### AGA rules

The American Go Association rules are area scoring by default, but are written so that territory-style counting, if used instead, is defined to produce the same result [@gomagic2026rulesets]. Standard komi is 7.5. Suicide is forbidden. AGA rules state an explicit **situational superko** rule: a move may not recreate a previous whole-board position with the same player to move next [@britgo2026compare].

### New Zealand rules

Area scoring, essentially Chinese rules with a handful of deliberate changes. The most notable is that a **multi-stone suicide** move — playing a stone that removes the last liberty from a group of two or more stones of your own color, without capturing anything — is legal. New Zealand rules are the rule set most often cited for this, alongside Ing rules [@britgo2026compare; @gokgs2026rulesets]. Standard komi is 7 points [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. New Zealand rules were also the first to write down an explicit situational superko rule, switching to it in 1978 after starting with positional superko in 1975 [@jasiek2026superko].

### Ing rules

Area scoring, but counted by a distinctive physical method: each player starts with exactly 180 stones, and after play both players fill their own remaining territory with their leftover stones, so the score can be read directly from how many stones are left over [@wikipedia2026ingrules]. Standard komi is stated as 8 points, but because Black wins any exact tie, the rule is effectively equivalent to a komi of 7.5 [@wikipedia2026ingrules; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Like New Zealand rules, Ing rules permit multi-stone suicide. Rather than a single superko statement, Ing rules distinguish a "fighting ko" from a "disturbing ko" and regulate each with its own timing restrictions [@wikipedia2026ingrules].

## Suicide: forbidden almost everywhere, legal in two rulesets

Playing a single stone onto a point where it would immediately have zero liberties and capture nothing is pointless under any rule set, so single-stone suicide almost never comes up as a live question. The real difference between rulesets is **multi-stone suicide**: a move that removes the last liberty of a larger friendly group without capturing anything. Japanese, Chinese, and AGA rules forbid this outright. New Zealand and Ing rules permit it [@britgo2026compare; @gokgs2026rulesets]. This mostly matters in rare, carefully constructed double-ko and multi-stone capturing race positions; it essentially never comes up in ordinary play, which is one reason many players go years without noticing which side of this rule their games are being played under.

## Ko and [superko](../../../glossary/terms/superko.md), in outline

Every ruleset above starts from the same simple [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) rule: a player may not immediately recapture a single stone if doing so would recreate the position from just before the opponent's last move. Where the rulesets differ is in how far that principle extends to rarer whole-board repetitions:

- Japanese and Korean rules mostly stop at the simple ko rule and traditionally treat other repeating cycles as an unresolved "no result."
- Chinese rules broadly forbid recreating any prior whole-board position.
- AGA and New Zealand rules state an explicit situational superko rule.
- Ing rules use a separate "fighting ko" versus "disturbing ko" distinction instead of a general superko statement.

This is a summary, not the full account. The mechanics of positional versus situational superko, and the rare board positions that expose the difference, belong to a dedicated lesson on [ko and superko](./ko-and-superko.md).

## What a beginner should actually do about all this

A beginner should pick whichever ruleset their club, teacher, or server already uses and not spend study time comparing rulesets further, for two reasons. First, as shown above, area and territory scoring agree on the winner in the overwhelming majority of finished games; the cases where they diverge (seki, disputed dead stones, rare multi-stone suicide positions) are advanced enough that a beginner is unlikely to produce one, let alone need to adjudicate one. Second, the skills that decide beginner-level games — reading captures, keeping groups alive, building territory — are identical under every ruleset described here. None of these rule sets changes how liberties, captures, or life and death work; they only change how the already-finished board gets turned into a final score.

Most online servers default to Chinese-style area scoring, and this is a practical choice rather than an aesthetic one. Because filling in your own territory costs nothing under area scoring, any disagreement about whether a group is alive or dead can be settled by simply resuming play and capturing it out, instead of requiring the players to negotiate an agreement before the count can happen. That makes area scoring far easier for software to enforce automatically without a human arbiter, which is exactly the situation an online server is in [@gomagic2026rulesets; @gokgs2026rulesets].

## Comparison table

| Ruleset | Scoring style | Standard komi | Suicide | Superko approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Japanese | Territory | 6.5 | Forbidden | Simple ko only; other repetitions traditionally "no result" |
| Korean | Territory | 6.5 | Forbidden | Simple ko; repeated whole-board positions are handled by a more explicitly written procedure than Japan's, but still end in a draw/"no result" if neither side breaks the cycle |
| Chinese | Area | 7.5 | Forbidden | Broad ban on recreating any prior whole-board position (positional-superko-like) |
| AGA | Area (defined to match territory counting) | 7.5 | Forbidden | Explicit situational superko |
| New Zealand | Area | 7 | Legal (multi-stone only) | Explicit situational superko (first ruleset to state one, switching from positional superko in 1978) |
| Ing | Area (counted via stone-filling) | 8, but Black wins ties (effectively 7.5) | Legal (multi-stone only) | "Fighting ko" vs. "disturbing ko" distinction, not a single superko rule |

## Exercises

1. Two players finish a game with no seki and no disputed dead stones. One count is done under Japanese territory rules, the other under Chinese area rules. Why should you expect the same player to win both counts?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because area scoring only adds the value of stones on the board on top of territory, and both players place roughly the same number of stones over the course of an ordinary game, including the dame-filling moves near the end. That extra value cancels out between the two players, so the margin between the two counting methods is usually zero or one point, not enough to flip the result outside unusual positions like seki or disputed dead stones.
</details>

2. A group is in seki. Why might a Chinese-rules count and a Japanese-rules count disagree about the score even though neither player captured anything?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Territory scoring gives no territory and no prisoners for a seki, since nothing was enclosed as territory and nothing was captured. Area scoring still counts every living stone in the seki as a point for its owner. If the two sides of the seki have an unequal number of stones, area scoring will show a different margin than territory scoring, even though the position and the set of living groups are identical under both rule sets.
</details>

3. Why do New Zealand and Ing rules allow multi-stone suicide when Japanese, Chinese, and AGA rules forbid it, and why does this rarely matter in practice?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

New Zealand and Ing rules were written to remove the suicide prohibition as an unnecessary special case rather than because suicide is normally useful; a legal multi-stone suicide move only changes the outcome of a small number of unusual double-ko or capturing-race positions. Because those positions are rare, most games played under any of these five rulesets would end identically whether or not multi-stone suicide were legal.
</details>

4. A beginner asks which ruleset they should learn first. What should they actually do, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Learn whichever ruleset their club, teacher, or server already uses, and stop worrying about the others. The differences between rulesets are almost entirely about how an already-finished position gets converted into a final score, not about how liberties, captures, or life and death work during play. A beginner's practical skills transfer completely across every ruleset described here.
</details>

## What comes next

Continue with [Ko and Superko](./ko-and-superko.md) for the detailed mechanics behind the summary above, including positional versus situational superko and the rare positions that expose the difference. For the scoring vocabulary this lesson depends on, see [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md) and the local [Terms](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md), especially [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md), [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md), and [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md).

rooms.title: area scoring
rooms.body:
Area scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the number of that player's own live stones remaining on the board plus the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md); captures made during play matter only insofar as they change which stones are on the board at the end, not as separately counted prisoner points [@britgo2025default]. Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules all use area scoring. Because a stone on the board and an enclosed empty point are worth the same one point each, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs nothing under area scoring: it simply converts a territory point into a stone point.

That single property is the main practical difference from [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md), and it is why area-scoring rulesets can set standard [komi](./komi.md) a half-point to a full point higher than territory-scoring rulesets covering the same game: Black, moving first, typically ends a game with one more stone on the board than White, and area scoring counts that stone directly where territory scoring would not. The exact standard komi for each ruleset is recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).

## Related terms

- [territory](./territory.md) - Area scoring counts a player's territory as part of the total, alongside that player's own stones.
- [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md) - Area scoring and territory scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.
- [komi](./komi.md) - Standard komi values differ between area-scoring and territory-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.
- [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) - Area-scoring rulesets typically resolve disputed dead stones by resuming play to an actual capture.
- [pass](./pass.md) - Some area-scoring implementations reconcile counts with territory scoring using a pass stone.

New Zealand Go Society, New Zealand Rules of Go

rooms.title: atari
rooms.description: Atari in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the state in which a stone or connected group has only one [liberty](./liberty.md) remaining and is therefore under immediate threat of [capture](./capture.md) [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].
rooms.body:
Atari in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the state in which a stone or connected group has only one [liberty](./liberty.md) remaining and is therefore under immediate threat of [capture](./capture.md) [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Atari matters because it turns a broad positional game into a forced tactical problem. When a group falls to one liberty, the next move often becomes urgent for both players: one side tries to capture, while the other tries to extend, connect, or create shape.

## Related terms

- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Atari is defined by the reduction to a single remaining liberty.
- [capture](./capture.md) - A capture follows if the threatened group cannot answer the atari.
- [connection](./connection.md) - Connecting to another group is one common way to escape atari.

rooms.title: capture
rooms.body:
A capture in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) occurs when a move removes the last [liberty](./liberty.md) from an opposing stone or connected group, after which those stones are removed from the board [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo].

Capture is the game's basic tactical enforcement rule. Without it, enclosure would carry no force. But weiqi is not a pure capture race, because players usually capture in order to secure shape, reduce influence, or stabilize [territory](./territory.md), not only to remove material.

## Related terms

- [atari](./atari.md) - Atari is the immediate threat state that often precedes capture.
- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Capture is defined by the removal of the last liberty.
- [life and death](./life-and-death.md) - Many life-and-death problems end by proving whether capture can be forced.
- [territory](./territory.md) - Captures often matter because they change which empty points can become territory.
- [ko](./ko.md) - Some captures trigger ko and cannot be answered by immediate recapture.

rooms.title: connection
rooms.description: A connection in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a relation between stones that makes them function as one group, sharing [liberties](./liberty.md) and supporting each other's defense [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].
rooms.body:
A connection in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a relation between stones that makes them function as one group, sharing [liberties](./liberty.md) and supporting each other's defense [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Connection is structurally important because isolated stones are weak. A move that does not gain immediate [territory](./territory.md) may still be strong if it joins two unsettled groups, prevents a cutting attack, or turns a fragile shape into one that can live.

## Related terms

- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Connected stones share liberties, which is why connection increases strength.
- [eye](./eye.md) - A connected group often tries to make eyes as one unit rather than as isolated stones.
- [life and death](./life-and-death.md) - Many life-and-death problems turn on whether stones can stay connected.

rooms.title: dame
rooms.description: Dame in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the neutral, empty points left on the board that border stones of both colors and belong to neither player's [territory](./territory.md) [@britgoagaexplain2026; @polgote2026rules].
rooms.body:
Dame in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the neutral, empty points left on the board that border stones of both colors and belong to neither player's [territory](./territory.md) [@britgoagaexplain2026; @polgote2026rules].

Whether it is worth spending a move to fill a dame depends entirely on which scoring system is being used, which is why the term matters more than its small size suggests. Under **area scoring** (the family that includes Chinese rules), the final count adds up living stones on the board plus surrounded territory. A stone played on a dame is a stone on the board, so it is worth exactly one point, the same as a stone played anywhere else legal. Leaving dame unfilled when the opponent can still fill them is therefore a real, countable loss [@britgoagaexplain2026].

Under **territory scoring** (the family that includes Japanese rules), the final count adds up vacant points enclosed as territory plus captured prisoners; stones on the board are not counted directly, and playing an extra stone inside one's own territory actually costs a point by removing a vacant point from the count. A dame is nobody's territory, so playing on one neither gains nor costs a point under this system — it is scored as if it never happened. Dame still get filled in practice, but for a different reason: filling them removes any ambiguity about where one player's wall ends and the other's begins, which is needed before the players can agree on the [territory](./territory.md) boundary at all [@polgote2026rules].

This difference is a common source of confusion for players who learn one ruleset and then watch or play under the other. A player used to area scoring may reflexively fill every last dame out of habit, which costs nothing under territory scoring but also gains nothing once the boundaries are already clear. A player used to territory scoring who switches to an area-scored game and treats dame as free points to skip will find those skipped points quietly go to the opponent instead.

## Related terms

- [pass](./pass.md) - Passing before all dame are filled can cost a point under area scoring, one reason passing is timed carefully.
- [territory](./territory.md) - Dame are defined by what they are not: nobody's secured territory.
- [komi](./komi.md) - Because komi is a fixed score adjustment, it does not change how dame are counted, only what the resulting total is compared against.
- [capture](./capture.md) - A dame can turn into a live point for one side if a nearby capture changes which stones actually stand.

Polgote, Go Rules: Japanese vs Chinese

rooms.title: dead stones
rooms.body:
Dead stones in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are stones left on the board after both players [pass](./pass.md) that cannot avoid eventual [capture](./capture.md) under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) reading always applies: it cannot make two secure [eyes](./eye.md) and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in [seki](./seki.md) and is never marked dead.

How dead stones are settled is one of the sharpest procedural differences between rulesets, and one the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) records explicitly. Japanese-style rules settle status by mutual agreement after the two passes, which is fast but is the classic source of scoring disputes when players disagree about a group's fate [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Chinese-style area-scoring play resolves genuine disagreements by resuming alternating play until the disputed group is actually captured or clearly alive, which is slower but leaves no room for disagreement about the result.

## Related terms

- [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) - A stone is dead exactly when life-and-death reading shows it cannot live.
- [pass](./pass.md) - Dead-stone settlement begins only after both players have passed in succession.
- [seki](./seki.md) - Stones in seki are explicitly not dead; they survive by sharing unfillable liberties.
- [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md) - Area-scoring rulesets typically settle disputed dead stones by resuming capture, not by agreement.
- [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md) - Territory-scoring rulesets typically settle dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.

Nihon Ki-in and Kansai Ki-in, The Japanese Rules of Go

rooms.title: eye
rooms.description: An eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an empty point or enclosed space inside a group's shape that functions as an internal [liberty](./liberty.md) and helps determine whether the group can live [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].
rooms.body:
An eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an empty point or enclosed space inside a group's shape that functions as an internal [liberty](./liberty.md) and helps determine whether the group can live [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Eyes matter because they change the status of a group. A surrounded group with no secure eye shape may still be dead, while a well-connected group with two separate eyes is usually safe. This is why players often defend shape even when no immediate [capture](./capture.md) is on the board.

## Related terms

- [liberty](./liberty.md) - An eye is a protected internal liberty.
- [connection](./connection.md) - Strong connection makes it easier for a group to form stable eyes.
- [life and death](./life-and-death.md) - Life-and-death reading asks whether a group can make enough eyes to survive.

rooms.title: false eye
rooms.description: A false eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an eye-shaped empty point that looks like a protected internal [liberty](./liberty.md) but does not meet the diagonal-control and connection requirements of a real [eye](./eye.md), so the opponent can eventually force the surrounding group to fill it [@senseislibrary2026falseeye].
rooms.body:
A false eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an eye-shaped empty point that looks like a protected internal [liberty](./liberty.md) but does not meet the diagonal-control and connection requirements of a real [eye](./eye.md), so the opponent can eventually force the surrounding group to fill it [@senseislibrary2026falseeye].

An eye stays real only if the stones around it are firmly connected and enough of the diagonal points next to it are also controlled by the same color: one diagonal for an eye in the corner, two on the edge, and three in the center of the board. A false eye fails one of these conditions. Often the surrounding stones can be cut apart, or too many of the diagonal points belong to the opponent. Once the opponent captures a cutting stone or occupies enough diagonals, the eye point stops being a safe internal liberty and becomes an ordinary point that the surrounding group may eventually have to fill itself, or that the opponent can play into without dying [@senseislibrary2026falseeye].

False eyes matter because they are easy to miscount during a fight. A group that appears to have two eyes may actually have one real eye and one false eye, which means it has only one secure eye and is not unconditionally alive. Reading whether an eye is true or false, especially in a group with a single large or oddly shaped internal space, is a core part of [life and death](./life-and-death.md) work: the difference between a true eye and a false eye is often the difference between a living group and a dead one.

## Related terms

- [eye](./eye.md) - A false eye is an eye-shaped point that fails the diagonal-control and connection tests that make a real eye secure.
- [life and death](./life-and-death.md) - Distinguishing true eyes from false eyes is a routine step in life-and-death reading.
- [connection](./connection.md) - A false eye often results from a weak connection among the stones that surround it.
- [liberty](./liberty.md) - A false eye is not a reliably protected liberty, unlike a true eye.

rooms.title: handicap
rooms.body:
A handicap in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a rule adjustment, usually extra Black stones placed before play begins, that lets players of unequal strength compete in a meaningful game [@britgo2026whatisgo; @britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Handicap is one reason weiqi supports play across large skill differences without becoming a different game. The stronger player does not receive more pieces or special powers during play. Instead, the weaker player begins from a materially stronger board position.

## Related terms

- [komi](./komi.md) - Komi balances even games, while handicap balances unequal players.
- [territory](./territory.md) - Handicap stones reshape the territorial balance from the first move.
- [connection](./connection.md) - Handicap stones are useful only if the weaker player can connect them into efficient whole-board structure.

British Go Association, How to Play Go

rooms.title: hoshi
rooms.description: Hoshi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen [@wikipedia2026handicap].
rooms.body:
Hoshi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen [@wikipedia2026handicap]. The nine points sit at the 4-4 point in each corner, the 4-10 point on the midpoint of each edge, and the 10-10 point at the exact center of the board [@wikipedia2026handicap].

Hoshi matter for two distinct reasons. First, they are the standard locations for handicap stones: the fixed Japanese placement pattern seats every handicap stone, from two up to nine, on one of these nine points, and the tengen point is the fifth and seventh stone added as handicaps increase (see [Handicap Placement and Komi Values](../../documents/articles/notes/handicap-placement-and-komi-values.md) for the full placement order). Second, even outside handicap games, the corner hoshi mark a natural opening frame: a stone on the 4-4 point does not by itself secure the corner the way a 3-3 point does, trading that immediate territory for speed and center-facing influence, which is why it is one of the most common corner openings for beginners to learn even though the 3-4 point (komoku) is usually described as the more evenly balanced choice between territory and influence [@nagofed2026thisisgo; @gomagic2026komoku].

Tengen, the center hoshi, is treated differently from the other eight points. Because it touches no edge or corner, a stone there does not immediately stake out enclosed territory the way a corner stone does, so professional players rarely open there in even games; it appears far more often as the fifth or seventh stone of a handicap setup, where it works with the surrounding corner and side stones already on the board rather than alone.

## Related terms

- [handicap](./handicap.md) - Hoshi are the fixed points on which handicap stones are placed.
- [komi](./komi.md) - Komi is the scoring counterpart to handicap placement on the hoshi.
- [territory](./territory.md) - A hoshi stone's opening value comes from how evenly it can grow into territory.

rooms.title: ko
rooms.description: Ko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition constraint that forbids a player from making the immediate recapture that would recreate the previous board position [@britgo2025default].
rooms.body:
Ko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition constraint that forbids a player from making the immediate recapture that would recreate the previous board position [@britgo2025default].

Ko matters because it prevents endless local loops while preserving the tactical possibility of capture. Once a ko appears, the fight usually stops being purely local: the blocked player must move elsewhere first, which can turn the rest of the board into leverage for the eventual return to the ko point.

## Related terms

- [superko](./superko.md) - Superko generalizes this simple ko rule to forbid recreating any earlier board position, not only the position from one move ago.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Ko arises from a specific kind of capture and attempted recapture.
- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Ko positions usually appear when liberties are reduced to a narrow exchange.
- [atari](./atari.md) - Many ko fights begin from repeated atari and recapture threats.
- [territory](./territory.md) - Ko fights often matter because the threatened capture would change important territory.

rooms.title: komi
rooms.description: Komi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo].
rooms.body:
Komi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo].

Komi matters because weiqi is asymmetrical at the start: Black moves first. Without compensation, that initiative would distort results across many even games. Komi is therefore a scoring adjustment, not a tactical rule inside local fights.

## Related terms

- [territory](./territory.md) - Komi is added during final scoring after territory and other points are counted.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Captures may affect the final score that komi then adjusts.
- [handicap](./handicap.md) - Handicap changes the starting position, while komi adjusts the score.

frontmatter.description: Komi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo].

rooms.title: liberty
rooms.body:
A liberty in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an empty intersection directly adjacent to a stone or connected group of stones [@nagofed2026thisisgo]. Liberties determine whether a group remains on the board. When the last liberty is removed, the group is subject to [capture](./capture.md).

Liberties matter because they convert board geometry into tactical pressure. A move may look quiet in territorial terms while still being urgent if it reduces a group from two liberties to one. This is why local fights in weiqi often turn on counting available adjacent points rather than on the nominal size of a group.

## Related terms

- [atari](./atari.md) - Atari is the urgent state in which only one liberty remains.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Capture happens when a stone or group loses its final liberty.
- [connection](./connection.md) - Connections matter because they let stones share liberties.
- [territory](./territory.md) - Securing territory often depends on keeping enough liberties to prevent invasion and capture.
- [ko](./ko.md) - Ko can arise when a single-stone capture would otherwise repeat because liberties are exchanged back and forth.

frontmatter.title: liberty
cites: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Go
North American Go Federation, This Is Go

rooms.title: life and death
rooms.body:
Life and death in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the analysis of whether a group can secure enough stable shape, usually through [eyes](./eye.md), to avoid [capture](./capture.md), or whether the opponent can force it off the board [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Life-and-death reading is one of the game's central skills because local shape decides global outcomes. A large territorial framework can collapse if one key group dies. A small group can become strategically decisive if it lives inside the opponent's area.

## Related terms

- [eye](./eye.md) - Eyes are the main structural feature used to determine whether a group lives.
- [connection](./connection.md) - Connected stones defend and build eye shape more effectively than scattered stones.
- [atari](./atari.md) - Atari is the immediate tactical pressure that often precedes life-and-death resolution.

rooms.title: pass
rooms.body:
A pass in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent [@britgo2025default]. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by [ko](./ko.md), [suicide](./suicide.md), or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture [@usgo2022agarules].

Passing is where the two major scoring conventions attach a small but real procedural difference. Under strict territory scoring, a pass costs nothing. Under some area-scoring implementations, and under the AGA's hybrid counting method specifically, each pass hands the opponent a stone (a "pass stone") to be placed in the passer's own territory before counting, which is precisely the device that keeps [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md) and [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md) results aligned [@usgo2022agarules].

## Related terms

- [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) - The pair of passes that ends play is what starts dead-stone settlement.
- [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md) - Some area-scoring implementations use a pass stone to keep area and territory counts consistent.
- [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md) - Territory scoring is the convention the pass stone device was designed to stay consistent with.
- [seki](./seki.md) - A seki is left unresolved through passing; neither side plays its shared liberties before the game ends.

frontmatter.title: pass
cites: British Go Association, A. Default Rules
American Go Association, AGA Rules of Go

rooms.title: seki
rooms.body:
Seki in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a standoff in which two or more groups of opposite color share their remaining [liberties](./liberty.md), and neither side can play into the shared liberties without reducing its own group to a liberty count the opponent can then capture on the next move [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Neither group has two [eyes](./eye.md), yet neither can be captured either, so both remain on the board unresolved for the rest of the game. Seki is a genuine third outcome for a local fight, distinct from either group living outright or dying.

Seki matters for scoring because it is handled differently, in detail, by different rulesets, which is exactly the kind of parameter the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) exists to pin down. Under territory scoring, the shared liberties inside a seki count as points for neither player and stones in seki earn no prisoner value, since nothing was captured. Under area scoring, each side's own stones in the seki count as that side's area as normal, while the shared liberties still count for neither side, since they are not enclosed exclusively by one color.

## Related terms

- [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) - Seki is the standoff outcome that arises specifically when neither side's life-and-death reading resolves in its favor.
- [eye](./eye.md) - Groups in seki characteristically lack the two eyes that would make them unconditionally alive.
- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Seki is defined by a shared, unfillable pool of liberties between opposing groups.
- [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md) - Area scoring counts each seki group's own stones but not the shared liberties between them.
- [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md) - Territory scoring credits neither side with the shared liberties inside a seki.

frontmatter.title: seki
cites: British Go Association, How to Play Go
Nihon Ki-in and Kansai Ki-in, The Japanese Rules of Go

rooms.title: suicide
rooms.body:
Suicide in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a move that would leave the moving player's own stone or group with zero [liberties](./liberty.md) after any opposing stones it removes are taken off the board [@britgo2025default]. Under most rulesets suicide is simply illegal: a player may not place a stone that reduces their own group to no liberties unless that same move first captures an opposing group and thereby restores at least one liberty. New Zealand rules are the well-known exception, permitting suicide of any size — a player may play a stone, or fill their own group's last liberties entirely, and the played stones are then immediately removed as self-captured [@nzgo2013rules].

Suicide is worth distinguishing carefully from an ordinary [capture](./capture.md) that happens to leave the capturing stone momentarily surrounded: legality is checked by removing captured opponent stones first, then checking the mover's own liberties, so a move that captures is never suicide even if, before the capture is applied, it looked like it had none. Suicide also differs from [ko](./ko.md): a ko recapture always removes exactly one opposing stone and is judged by the repetition rule, while suicide by definition captures nothing at all.

## Related terms

- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Suicide is defined directly in terms of a move reducing the mover's own liberties to zero.
- [capture](./capture.md) - A move is never suicide if it captures an opposing group first, since capture is checked before self-liberties.
- [eye](./eye.md) - Rulesets that forbid suicide are the reason a genuine single-point eye cannot legally be filled by the opponent without first capturing around it.
- [ko](./ko.md) - Ko recaptures and suicide are easy to confuse; ko always captures one stone, suicide by definition captures none.

frontmatter.title: suicide
cites: British Go Association, A. Default Rules
New Zealand Go Society, New Zealand Rules of Go

rooms.title: superko
rooms.body:
Superko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition rule that extends [ko](./ko.md) beyond the single immediately-preceding position: it forbids recreating *any* whole-board position that has already occurred in the game, not only the one position just before the opponent's last move [@britgo2025default]. Two variants are in common use. Positional superko (PSK) forbids any recurrence of an identical arrangement of stones, regardless of whose turn it is. Situational superko (SSK) forbids a recurrence only when it is also the same player's turn to move as it was the earlier time that arrangement occurred — so the same stone arrangement may legally recur once with the other player to move, but not a second time with the original player to move [@usgo2022agarules].

Superko matters because the simple ko rule alone only blocks immediate two-move recaptures; it does nothing to stop longer cycles, such as triple ko or other multi-ko patterns, from repeating a board position indefinitely and preventing the game from ever concluding. Superko rules close that gap by treating repetition of the whole board, not just of one local point, as the thing to forbid. Which variant a ruleset adopts is one of the parameters recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md), since Chinese-tradition and New Zealand rules typically use positional superko while AGA rules specify situational superko, and Japanese rules historically rely on simple ko alone plus an ad hoc "no result" convention for unresolved long cycles.

## Related terms

- [ko](./ko.md) - Superko generalizes the simple ko rule from one forbidden position to all previously occurring positions.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Superko violations can only arise from sequences of captures and recaptures, since placement alone never restores an earlier board.
- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Long ko cycles that superko must adjudicate arise from groups repeatedly reduced to and restored from a shared last liberty.
- [seki](./seki.md) - Some multi-ko fights that superko must resolve are closely related to seki: neither side can safely play the deciding capture.

frontmatter.title: superko
cites: British Go Association, A. Default Rules
American Go Association, AGA Rules of Go
New Zealand Go Society, New Zealand Rules of Go

rooms.title: territory scoring
rooms.body:
Territory scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md) plus the prisoners that player captured from the opponent during the game; a live stone remaining on the board at the end contributes no direct point value of its own [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Japanese and Korean rules use territory scoring. Because stones themselves are not counted, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs a full point under territory scoring: it removes one territory point and, since nothing was captured, adds nothing back.

That cost is the main practical difference from [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md), and it is one reason experienced players under territory scoring stop playing inside their own territory as soon as a group is settled, while players under area scoring can fill such points for free. The exact standard komi and other parameters for each ruleset are recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).

## Related terms

- [territory](./territory.md) - Territory scoring's core term is the vacant points a player's stones enclose.
- [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md) - Territory scoring and area scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.
- [komi](./komi.md) - Standard komi values differ between territory-scoring and area-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.
- [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) - Territory-scoring rulesets typically resolve dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Captures matter directly under territory scoring, since prisoners are added to the final count.

frontmatter.title: territory scoring
cites: Nihon Ki-in and Kansai Ki-in, The Japanese Rules of Go
British Go Association, A. Default Rules

rooms.title: territory
rooms.body:
Territory in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the set of vacant points effectively enclosed by one player's stones and unavailable to the opponent except at unacceptable cost [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo].

Territory is the strategic heart of the game because it turns placement into scoring. A move may increase territory directly by closing space, or indirectly by making an invasion weak. This is why players often choose moves that neither attack nor defend a single group immediately but instead reshape the balance of large empty regions.

## Related terms

- [liberty](./liberty.md) - Territory remains meaningful only if the surrounding stones retain enough liberties to hold it.
- [capture](./capture.md) - Captures can secure or destroy territory by changing which stones remain on the board.
- [komi](./komi.md) - Komi adjusts final scores after territory has been counted.
- [ko](./ko.md) - Ko fights can determine whether a key territorial area remains secure.

frontmatter.title: territory
cites: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Go
North American Go Federation, This Is Go

rooms.body:
# Weiqi

Weiqi is a domain within Board Games.

This page is the start-here index for everything this section holds about weiqi — the sequenced lesson curriculum and the dependency-linked glossary — per the [Weiqi Platform Plan](../../documents/articles/notes/weiqi-platform-plan.md)'s "engine is the executable form of the glossary" thesis.

## Lessons

Read in this order; each lesson names what comes next.

1. [Weiqi Overview](../../documents/articles/notes/weiqi-overview.md) — liberties, capture, territory, and ko, via one worked example.
2. [Living Groups and Eyes](../../documents/articles/notes/living-groups-and-eyes.md) — why connection and eye shape determine whether a group lives or dies.
3. [Komi and Handicap](../../documents/articles/notes/komi-and-handicap.md) — how even games and uneven games are balanced.
4. [Ending the Game](../../documents/articles/notes/ending-the-game.md) — passing, dead-stone settlement, scoring both ways, and why area and territory rarely differ.
5. [History of Weiqi](../../documents/articles/notes/weiqi-history.md) — origins in China, transmission across East Asia, and modern international play. (A parallel entry, not a prerequisite for the other four.)

## Terms

Seventeen dependency-linked terms in four clusters.

**Tactical** — liberty, atari, capture, ko, superko, suicide:

- [liberty](../terms/liberty.md)
- [atari](../terms/atari.md)
- [capture](../terms/capture.md)
- [ko](../terms/ko.md)
- [superko](../terms/superko.md)
- [suicide](../terms/suicide.md)

**Scoring** — territory, komi, handicap, area scoring, territory scoring, pass, dead stones:

- [territory](../terms/territory.md)
- [komi](../terms/komi.md)
- [handicap](../terms/handicap.md)
- [area scoring](../terms/area-scoring.md)
- [territory scoring](../terms/territory-scoring.md)
- [pass](../terms/pass.md)
- [dead stones](../terms/dead-stones.md)

**Structural** — connection, eye, life-and-death, seki:

- [connection](../terms/connection.md)
- [eye](../terms/eye.md)
- [life and death](../terms/life-and-death.md)
- [seki](../terms/seki.md)

## Other section content

- [Provenance Policy](../../documents/articles/notes/provenance-policy.md) — how this section marks historical and superseded documents.
- [Weiqi Platform Plan](../../documents/articles/notes/weiqi-platform-plan.md) — the governing plan for the weiqi web platform build.
- [Rulesets](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) — ko regime, suicide, scoring, komi, and handicap placement compared across Chinese, Japanese, AGA, New Zealand, and Ing play, with stable identifiers for the kernel.
- [Regression Positions](../../documents/articles/notes/regression-positions.md) — thirteen small, labeled board positions seeding the rules kernel's test corpus.

A [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) is a player declining to place a stone on their turn. It is, instead, a statement that, in the passing player's judgment, no move remains that would improve their position. This lesson assumes the conceptual distinction covered in [Komi and Handicap](./komi-and-handicap.md): komi is a scoring offset for an even game, handicap is a positional offset for an unequal one. Two players want a fair game. One is 5 kyu, the other 1 kyu. The rank gap is four grades, so the rule of thumb calls for a four-stone handicap [@britgo2026rating]. The weaker player, 5 kyu, takes Black and places four stones before White's first move, on the four corner [hoshi](../../../glossary/terms/hoshi.md): the two diagonal corners used for a two-stone handicap, plus the third and fourth corners added in sequence [@wikipedia2026handicap]. Because this is a handicap game rather than an even game, White does not receive the usual 6 to 7 and a half point komi; instead, under Japanese rules (assumed here), the game is played at a nominal 0.5 komi, just enough to prevent a drawn result [@wikipedia2026komi]. Not every ruleset stops there — see the komi table below for the additional stone-scaled compensation Chinese and AGA rules add on top of that 0.5. If the two players later find the four-stone game one-sided, the standard adjustment is to change the stone count by one rather than to tune komi, since komi is calibrated for near-equal strength, not for large rank gaps.

In an even game, Black moves first and White receives [komi](../../../glossary/terms/komi.md), a fixed score bonus that offsets the first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo]. In a teaching game between players of unequal strength, the weaker player may instead receive [handicap](../../../glossary/terms/handicap.md) stones before play begins [@britgo2026whatisgo]. These two adjustments solve different problems. Komi balances the initiative inside an otherwise equal game. Handicap balances the starting position between unequal players.

Imagine Black has enclosed a small corner group so that two separate empty points remain inside its shape. White surrounds the outside completely. Even so, Black's group is usually safe. White cannot simply fill both internal points in sequence, because each point functions as an [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md), and the group remains alive as long as those internal liberties stay structurally separate [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

A [connection](../../../glossary/terms/connection.md) turns separate stones into one unit. That matters because connected stones share [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md), answer attacks together, and can build internal shape more efficiently than isolated stones can [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. Many local fights are therefore really fights over cutting and connecting.

That matters because connected stones share [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md), answer attacks together, and can build internal shape more efficiently than isolated stones can [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. Many local fights are therefore really fights over cutting and connecting.

When a player connects two weak stones, the move may look passive. But it often changes the status of the whole position. A connected group may escape [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md), threaten to make eyes, or stop the opponent from splitting the board into easy targets.

The usual practical rule is simple: a group with two secure eyes lives, while a group that cannot make two eyes may die [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. This is the core of [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md). Players read local sequences to determine whether a group can form those eyes before the opponent seals it in.

Life-and-death judgment is not a narrow endgame skill. It changes strategic value across the whole board. A move that saves a living group can preserve a large territorial framework. A move that kills an invading group can turn a contested region into secure [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md).

Each cell above is addressable as `ruleset.<name>.<parameter>`, matching the [ontology](../../../glossary/topics/weiqi.md)'s intent that the engine be the executable form of the glossary. The five ruleset names are `chinese`, `japanese`, `aga`, `newzealand`, `ing`. The five parameter names, and the value vocabulary each one draws from, are:

**Ko regime.** [Simple ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) forbids only the single immediate recapture; it is the shared baseline every ruleset here includes. [Superko](../../../glossary/terms/superko.md) extends that ban to any repeated whole-board position. Japanese rules are the outlier: they specify no formal superko rule at all, relying instead on the two-pass-and-agree convention for ordinary games and a "no result" (rematch) ruling for the rare unresolved long cycle such as triple ko [@nihonkiin1989rules]. AGA rules specify situational superko explicitly [@usgo2022agarules]; Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules are generally implemented with positional superko in modern digital play, though traditional over-the-board Chinese rules historically left long cycles to ad hoc agreement much like Japanese rules do [@britgo2025default]. A kernel targeting strict traditional Chinese play should treat `ruleset.chinese.ko_regime` as configurable rather than fixed.

**Scoring.** [Area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md) counts stones plus territory; [territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md) counts territory plus prisoners only. AGA rules are unusual in supporting both, reconciled so the two counts normally agree via the pass-stone convention described in [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) [@usgo2022agarules].

**Scoring.** [Area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md) counts stones plus territory; [territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md) counts territory plus prisoners only. AGA rules are unusual in supporting both, reconciled so the two counts normally agree via the pass-stone convention described in [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) [@usgo2022agarules].

**Scoring.** [Area scoring](../../../glossary/terms/area-scoring.md) counts stones plus territory; [territory scoring](../../../glossary/terms/territory-scoring.md) counts territory plus prisoners only. AGA rules are unusual in supporting both, reconciled so the two counts normally agree via the pass-stone convention described in [pass](../../../glossary/terms/pass.md) [@usgo2022agarules].

**Standard komi.** Values above are the modern standard for an even game with no handicap; historical values have differed (Japanese komi was commonly 5.5 before a widely-adopted 2002 shift to 6.5, and Chinese komi has likewise moved between 5.5, 7.5, and other values across the twentieth century) [@britannica2026go]. The roughly one-point gap between Chinese-style area komi (7.5) and Japanese territory komi (6.5) is not arbitrary: it approximates the systematic scoring difference explained in [Ending the Game](./ending-the-game.md#why-area-and-territory-rarely-differ), where area scoring credits Black with one extra stone that territory scoring does not. Ing komi (8) reflects a separately-set tradition rather than the same offset logic.

Imagine a small region near the side of the board where a Black group and a White group are packed against each other and against the edge. Both groups are otherwise completely enclosed, connected to nothing else alive elsewhere on the board, and neither has an [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md) of its own. Between the two groups sit exactly two empty points, side by side, and those two points are the only [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md) either group has left.

Imagine a small region near the side of the board where a Black group and a White group are packed against each other and against the edge. Both groups are otherwise completely enclosed, connected to nothing else alive elsewhere on the board, and neither has an [eye](../../../glossary/terms/eye.md) of its own. Between the two groups sit exactly two empty points, side by side, and those two points are the only [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md) either group has left.

Neither player can safely act on those two points. If Black plays on one of them, Black fills one of Black's own group's last two liberties, along with one of White's, and Black's group drops to a single liberty: [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md). White then plays the remaining shared point and captures the entire Black group. The same logic runs in reverse if White moves first: White's group ends up in atari, and Black captures. Because moving first into the shared space is always worse than leaving it alone, neither player ever plays there, and the position holds for the rest of the game. This is [seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md): both groups stay on the board, alive, without either one ever forming two separate eyes.

Now imagine a Black group that has enclosed a single empty point in what looks like a normal eye: the point itself is empty, and every intersection directly orthogonal to it is a Black stone. This point sits on the first line, directly along the side of the board (not in a corner). But of the diagonal points next to it, only one is Black, and that stone is a lone stone with few liberties of its own and no solid [connection](../../../glossary/terms/connection.md) to the rest of the group. The other relevant diagonal belongs to White.

An eye's security depends on more than its four orthogonal neighbors. The defending color also needs to control enough of the diagonal points around it: one diagonal if the eye sits in a corner, two if it sits on an edge, and three if it sits in the middle of the board [@senseislibrary2026falseeye]. This eye is on the edge, so Black needs two secure diagonals and has only one, and that one is itself capturable. If White captures the weak diagonal stone, White gets a stone directly next to the eye point. The point is then no longer surrounded solely by connected Black stones, so White can play into it. That makes this a [false eye](../../../glossary/terms/false-eye.md): a point that currently looks like a second eye but can eventually be forced open.

If this is the only other candidate eye the group has besides one genuine eye elsewhere, the group does not have two real eyes yet. Under ordinary [life and death](../../../glossary/terms/life-and-death.md) reading, one true eye plus one false eye counts as one eye, not two, and a group with only one secure eye is not unconditionally alive. It survives only if it can still make a second true eye somewhere else, or if the surrounding position turns into a capturing race or a seki instead.

Seki and false eyes are both exceptions to the simple version of "two eyes live" introduced in [Living Groups and Eyes](./living-groups-and-eyes.md), so it is worth rereading that lesson's eye-shape discussion once these two ideas are clear. **Founding incident.** On 2026-08-19 — the same day [Regression Positions](./regression-positions.md) was authored — that document's own R9 diagram (the area-score worked example) and its `expected:` block briefly disagreed with each other during authoring: the diagram is the source of truth, and its stone counts, territory counts, and area scores must be *derivable* from it, not merely asserted beside it. The disagreement was caught only because a human re-derived the arithmetic by hand before the position was trusted as a kernel regression fixture — not because any automated process read the diagram, replayed or recomputed it, and checked the `expected:` block's numbers against that computation. No such process existed. `weiqi-kernel`'s own test suite (`apps/weiqi-kernel/test/scoring.test.mts`) now encodes R9 correctly, transcribed by hand a second time by a careful implementer — but the corpus document itself has no standing guarantee that its *next* edit won't reintroduce the same class of slip, silently, since nothing reads `regression-positions.md` and checks it against `weiqi-kernel` the way `weiqi-kernel`'s tests check themselves against it. This is exactly the gap `weiqi-lsp` exists to close, and it is the incident this record's board authorization (below) points to as concrete evidence for what the plan's own regression-corpus clause already anticipated in the abstract.

Imagine an empty 9 by 9 board. Black places one stone near the center. White then places stones on each of the four adjacent intersections around it. Once Black's stone has no remaining [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md), White removes it from the board. That is a [capture](../../../glossary/terms/capture.md).

Imagine an empty 9 by 9 board. Black places one stone near the center. White then places stones on each of the four adjacent intersections around it. Once Black's stone has no remaining [liberties](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md), White removes it from the board. That is a [capture](../../../glossary/terms/capture.md).

The central tactical unit is the liberty. A single stone in open space has four liberties, fewer on the edge, and fewer again in the corner. Connected stones share liberties, which is why groups matter more than isolated stones. When a move removes the last liberty from an opposing stone or group, the player captures it and removes it from the board [@nagofed2026thisisgo]. A stone or group reduced to one liberty is in [atari](../../../glossary/terms/atari.md), which is the game's simplest tactical alarm.

The strategic objective is [territory](../../../glossary/terms/territory.md), not only capture. Players try to secure vacant points by surrounding them more solidly than the opponent can invade or reduce [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo]. This is why a move that does not capture anything immediately can still be strong: it may stabilize a large territorial framework or prevent the opponent from doing so.

The game also needs a rule to prevent immediate infinite repetition. That rule is [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md): after a capture that would allow the opponent to recreate the exact previous board position with one move, that immediate recapture is forbidden [@britgo2025default]. Ko turns some local fights into timing problems that reach across the whole board, because the player who is blocked from recapturing must play elsewhere first.

Across a full game, both players place roughly the same number of stones, including the neutral endgame points ([dame](../../../glossary/terms/dame.md)) that get filled in near the close of play. Area scoring pays a point for every stone on the board, including those dame-filling moves; territory scoring pays nothing for them. As long as both sides fill roughly equal numbers of dame points, that difference cancels out between the two players, leaving the margin between area and territory results at zero or one point [@britgo2026compare].

- **[Seki](../../../glossary/terms/seki.md)** (a mutual standoff where neither side can profitably capture the other). Territory scoring gives no territory and no prisoners to either seki group, since nothing was captured and no space was ever "enclosed" territory. Area scoring still counts each living stone in the seki, so an uneven number of stones on each side of a seki can shift the count by a few points under area rules where it would not move at all under territory rules [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets].

Territory scoring; standard even-game komi is 6.5 points [@britgo2026compare; @gomagic2026rulesets]. Suicide (playing a stone with no remaining [liberty](../../../glossary/terms/liberty.md) that captures nothing) is forbidden. Only the simple [ko](../../../glossary/terms/ko.md) rule — no immediate one-move recapture that restores the prior position — is written into the rules; broader repeating whole-board positions have traditionally been ruled "no result," requiring the game to be replayed, rather than resolved by a general superko rule [@britgo2026compare].

Area scoring counts a player's territory as part of the total, alongside that player's own stones.
Area scoring and territory scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.
Standard komi values differ between area-scoring and territory-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.
Area-scoring rulesets typically resolve disputed dead stones by resuming play to an actual capture.
Some area-scoring implementations reconcile counts with territory scoring using a pass stone.

Area scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the number of that player's own live stones remaining on the board plus the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md); captures made during play matter only insofar as they change which stones are on the board at the end, not as separately counted prisoner points [@britgo2025default]. Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules all use area scoring. Because a stone on the board and an enclosed empty point are worth the same one point each, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs nothing under area scoring: it simply converts a territory point into a stone point.

That single property is the main practical difference from [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md), and it is why area-scoring rulesets can set standard [komi](./komi.md) a half-point to a full point higher than territory-scoring rulesets covering the same game: Black, moving first, typically ends a game with one more stone on the board than White, and area scoring counts that stone directly where territory scoring would not. The exact standard komi for each ruleset is recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).
Atari is defined by the reduction to a single remaining liberty.
A capture follows if the threatened group cannot answer the atari.
Connecting to another group is one common way to escape atari.

Atari in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the state in which a stone or connected group has only one [liberty](./liberty.md) remaining and is therefore under immediate threat of [capture](./capture.md) [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].
Atari is the immediate threat state that often precedes capture.
Capture is defined by the removal of the last liberty.
Many life-and-death problems end by proving whether capture can be forced.
Captures often matter because they change which empty points can become territory.
Some captures trigger ko and cannot be answered by immediate recapture.

A capture in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) occurs when a move removes the last [liberty](./liberty.md) from an opposing stone or connected group, after which those stones are removed from the board [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo].
Connected stones share liberties, which is why connection increases strength.
A connected group often tries to make eyes as one unit rather than as isolated stones.
Many life-and-death problems turn on whether stones can stay connected.

A connection in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a relation between stones that makes them function as one group, sharing [liberties](./liberty.md) and supporting each other's defense [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Connection is structurally important because isolated stones are weak. A move that does not gain immediate [territory](./territory.md) may still be strong if it joins two unsettled groups, prevents a cutting attack, or turns a fragile shape into one that can live.
Passing before all dame are filled can cost a point under area scoring, one reason passing is timed carefully.
Dame are defined by what they are not: nobody's secured territory.
Because komi is a fixed score adjustment, it does not change how dame are counted, only what the resulting total is compared against.
A dame can turn into a live point for one side if a nearby capture changes which stones actually stand.

Dame in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the neutral, empty points left on the board that border stones of both colors and belong to neither player's [territory](./territory.md) [@britgoagaexplain2026; @polgote2026rules].
A stone is dead exactly when life-and-death reading shows it cannot live.
Dead-stone settlement begins only after both players have passed in succession.
Stones in seki are explicitly not dead; they survive by sharing unfillable liberties.
Area-scoring rulesets typically settle disputed dead stones by resuming capture, not by agreement.
Territory-scoring rulesets typically settle dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.

Dead stones in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are stones left on the board after both players [pass](./pass.md) that cannot avoid eventual [capture](./capture.md) under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) reading always applies: it cannot make two secure [eyes](./eye.md) and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in [seki](./seki.md) and is never marked dead.
