Dead stones in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are stones left on the board after both players [pass](./pass.md) that cannot avoid eventual [capture](./capture.md) under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) reading always applies: it cannot make two secure [eyes](./eye.md) and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in [seki](./seki.md) and is never marked dead.

How dead stones are settled is one of the sharpest procedural differences between rulesets, and one the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) records explicitly. Japanese-style rules settle status by mutual agreement after the two passes, which is fast but is the classic source of scoring disputes when players disagree about a group's fate [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Chinese-style area-scoring play resolves genuine disagreements by resuming alternating play until the disputed group is actually captured or clearly alive, which is slower but leaves no room for disagreement about the result.
An eye is a protected internal liberty.
Strong connection makes it easier for a group to form stable eyes.
Life-and-death reading asks whether a group can make enough eyes to survive.

An eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an empty point or enclosed space inside a group's shape that functions as an internal [liberty](./liberty.md) and helps determine whether the group can live [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Eyes matter because they change the status of a group. A surrounded group with no secure eye shape may still be dead, while a well-connected group with two separate eyes is usually safe. This is why players often defend shape even when no immediate [capture](./capture.md) is on the board.
A false eye is an eye-shaped point that fails the diagonal-control and connection tests that make a real eye secure.
Distinguishing true eyes from false eyes is a routine step in life-and-death reading.
A false eye often results from a weak connection among the stones that surround it.
A false eye is not a reliably protected liberty, unlike a true eye.

A false eye in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an eye-shaped empty point that looks like a protected internal [liberty](./liberty.md) but does not meet the diagonal-control and connection requirements of a real [eye](./eye.md), so the opponent can eventually force the surrounding group to fill it [@senseislibrary2026falseeye].
Komi balances even games, while handicap balances unequal players.
Handicap stones reshape the territorial balance from the first move.
Handicap stones are useful only if the weaker player can connect them into efficient whole-board structure.

A handicap in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a rule adjustment, usually extra Black stones placed before play begins, that lets players of unequal strength compete in a meaningful game [@britgo2026whatisgo; @britgo2026howtoplaygo].
Hoshi are the fixed points on which handicap stones are placed.
Komi is the scoring counterpart to handicap placement on the hoshi.
A hoshi stone's opening value comes from how evenly it can grow into territory.

Hoshi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen [@wikipedia2026handicap]. The nine points sit at the 4-4 point in each corner, the 4-10 point on the midpoint of each edge, and the 10-10 point at the exact center of the board [@wikipedia2026handicap].

Hoshi matter for two distinct reasons. First, they are the standard locations for handicap stones: the fixed Japanese placement pattern seats every handicap stone, from two up to nine, on one of these nine points, and the tengen point is the fifth and seventh stone added as handicaps increase (see [Handicap Placement and Komi Values](../../documents/articles/notes/handicap-placement-and-komi-values.md) for the full placement order). Second, even outside handicap games, the corner hoshi mark a natural opening frame: a stone on the 4-4 point does not by itself secure the corner the way a 3-3 point does, trading that immediate territory for speed and center-facing influence, which is why it is one of the most common corner openings for beginners to learn even though the 3-4 point (komoku) is usually described as the more evenly balanced choice between territory and influence [@nagofed2026thisisgo; @gomagic2026komoku].
Superko generalizes this simple ko rule to forbid recreating any earlier board position, not only the position from one move ago.
Ko arises from a specific kind of capture and attempted recapture.
Ko positions usually appear when liberties are reduced to a narrow exchange.
Many ko fights begin from repeated atari and recapture threats.
Ko fights often matter because the threatened capture would change important territory.
Ko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition constraint that forbids a player from making the immediate recapture that would recreate the previous board position [@britgo2025default].
Komi is added during final scoring after territory and other points are counted.
Captures may affect the final score that komi then adjusts.
Handicap changes the starting position, while komi adjusts the score.
Komi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage [@britgo2025default; @britgo2026whatisgo].
Atari is the urgent state in which only one liberty remains.
Capture happens when a stone or group loses its final liberty.
Connections matter because they let stones share liberties.
Securing territory often depends on keeping enough liberties to prevent invasion and capture.
Ko can arise when a single-stone capture would otherwise repeat because liberties are exchanged back and forth.

A liberty in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is an empty intersection directly adjacent to a stone or connected group of stones [@nagofed2026thisisgo]. Liberties determine whether a group remains on the board. When the last liberty is removed, the group is subject to [capture](./capture.md).
Eyes are the main structural feature used to determine whether a group lives.
Connected stones defend and build eye shape more effectively than scattered stones.
Atari is the immediate tactical pressure that often precedes life-and-death resolution.

Life and death in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the analysis of whether a group can secure enough stable shape, usually through [eyes](./eye.md), to avoid [capture](./capture.md), or whether the opponent can force it off the board [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].

Life and death in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the analysis of whether a group can secure enough stable shape, usually through [eyes](./eye.md), to avoid [capture](./capture.md), or whether the opponent can force it off the board [@britgo2026howtoplaygo].
The pair of passes that ends play is what starts dead-stone settlement.
Some area-scoring implementations use a pass stone to keep area and territory counts consistent.
Territory scoring is the convention the pass stone device was designed to stay consistent with.
A seki is left unresolved through passing; neither side plays its shared liberties before the game ends.

A pass in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent [@britgo2025default]. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by [ko](./ko.md), [suicide](./suicide.md), or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture [@usgo2022agarules].

A pass in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent [@britgo2025default]. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by [ko](./ko.md), [suicide](./suicide.md), or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture [@usgo2022agarules].

A pass in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent [@britgo2025default]. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by [ko](./ko.md), [suicide](./suicide.md), or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture [@usgo2022agarules].
Seki is the standoff outcome that arises specifically when neither side's life-and-death reading resolves in its favor.
Groups in seki characteristically lack the two eyes that would make them unconditionally alive.
Seki is defined by a shared, unfillable pool of liberties between opposing groups.
Area scoring counts each seki group's own stones but not the shared liberties between them.
Territory scoring credits neither side with the shared liberties inside a seki.

Seki in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a standoff in which two or more groups of opposite color share their remaining [liberties](./liberty.md), and neither side can play into the shared liberties without reducing its own group to a liberty count the opponent can then capture on the next move [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Neither group has two [eyes](./eye.md), yet neither can be captured either, so both remain on the board unresolved for the rest of the game. Seki is a genuine third outcome for a local fight, distinct from either group living outright or dying.

Seki matters for scoring because it is handled differently, in detail, by different rulesets, which is exactly the kind of parameter the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) exists to pin down. Under territory scoring, the shared liberties inside a seki count as points for neither player and stones in seki earn no prisoner value, since nothing was captured. Under area scoring, each side's own stones in the seki count as that side's area as normal, while the shared liberties still count for neither side, since they are not enclosed exclusively by one color.
Suicide is defined directly in terms of a move reducing the mover's own liberties to zero.
A move is never suicide if it captures an opposing group first, since capture is checked before self-liberties.
Rulesets that forbid suicide are the reason a genuine single-point eye cannot legally be filled by the opponent without first capturing around it.
Ko recaptures and suicide are easy to confuse; ko always captures one stone, suicide by definition captures none.

Suicide in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a move that would leave the moving player's own stone or group with zero [liberties](./liberty.md) after any opposing stones it removes are taken off the board [@britgo2025default]. Under most rulesets suicide is simply illegal: a player may not place a stone that reduces their own group to no liberties unless that same move first captures an opposing group and thereby restores at least one liberty. New Zealand rules are the well-known exception, permitting suicide of any size — a player may play a stone, or fill their own group's last liberties entirely, and the played stones are then immediately removed as self-captured [@nzgo2013rules].
Superko generalizes the simple ko rule from one forbidden position to all previously occurring positions.
Superko violations can only arise from sequences of captures and recaptures, since placement alone never restores an earlier board.
Long ko cycles that superko must adjudicate arise from groups repeatedly reduced to and restored from a shared last liberty.
Some multi-ko fights that superko must resolve are closely related to seki: neither side can safely play the deciding capture.

Superko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition rule that extends [ko](./ko.md) beyond the single immediately-preceding position: it forbids recreating *any* whole-board position that has already occurred in the game, not only the one position just before the opponent's last move [@britgo2025default]. Two variants are in common use. Positional superko (PSK) forbids any recurrence of an identical arrangement of stones, regardless of whose turn it is. Situational superko (SSK) forbids a recurrence only when it is also the same player's turn to move as it was the earlier time that arrangement occurred — so the same stone arrangement may legally recur once with the other player to move, but not a second time with the original player to move [@usgo2022agarules].

Superko matters because the simple ko rule alone only blocks immediate two-move recaptures; it does nothing to stop longer cycles, such as triple ko or other multi-ko patterns, from repeating a board position indefinitely and preventing the game from ever concluding. Superko rules close that gap by treating repetition of the whole board, not just of one local point, as the thing to forbid. Which variant a ruleset adopts is one of the parameters recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md), since Chinese-tradition and New Zealand rules typically use positional superko while AGA rules specify situational superko, and Japanese rules historically rely on simple ko alone plus an ad hoc "no result" convention for unresolved long cycles.
Territory scoring's core term is the vacant points a player's stones enclose.
Territory scoring and area scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.
Standard komi values differ between territory-scoring and area-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.
Territory-scoring rulesets typically resolve dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.
Captures matter directly under territory scoring, since prisoners are added to the final count.

Territory scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md) plus the prisoners that player captured from the opponent during the game; a live stone remaining on the board at the end contributes no direct point value of its own [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Japanese and Korean rules use territory scoring. Because stones themselves are not counted, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs a full point under territory scoring: it removes one territory point and, since nothing was captured, adds nothing back.

That cost is the main practical difference from [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md), and it is one reason experienced players under territory scoring stop playing inside their own territory as soon as a group is settled, while players under area scoring can fill such points for free. The exact standard komi and other parameters for each ruleset are recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).
Territory remains meaningful only if the surrounding stones retain enough liberties to hold it.
Captures can secure or destroy territory by changing which stones remain on the board.
Komi adjusts final scores after territory has been counted.
Ko fights can determine whether a key territorial area remains secure.

Territory in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the set of vacant points effectively enclosed by one player's stones and unavailable to the opponent except at unacceptable cost [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo].

cards.front: A player passes on move 140, then immediately regrets it because a large dame point is still open. Under area scoring, what does that pass cost them, and why would the same pass cost nothing under most forms of territory scoring?
cards.back: Under area scoring, every stone on the board counts toward the final score, so leaving a fillable dame for the opponent to take is a real, one-point loss. Under territory scoring, dame are not counted at all — filling them establishes boundaries but does not add to either player's score — so passing before they are filled changes nothing about the count, even though it may still trigger settlement earlier than the player wanted.

cards.front: Two players pass, then disagree about whether a five-stone group in the corner is dead. Under the AGA-style default rules, who gets to move first when play resumes, and what ends the game for good this time?
cards.back: The opponent of whichever player passed last gets the next move. The game ends for good either when the players reach agreement on the group's status, or when both players pass twice again in succession, at which point any stones still on the board are simply ruled alive.

cards.front: Why does an online server's "auto-score" or score-estimator button need a human override, instead of just deciding the game automatically?
cards.back: Automated estimators are good at obvious cases but can misjudge close life-and-death situations, seki, or unusual dame configurations. Because the final result is often locked in permanently once accepted, servers let players correct the estimate — or cancel and resume play entirely — rather than trusting the automation to settle a genuinely disputed group.

cards.front: Why doesn't a pass ever violate the ko rule, no matter what ko fights are active on the board?
cards.back: Because a pass places no stone and changes nothing about the board. The ko rule only restricts moves that would recreate a previous position; a pass cannot recreate anything, since it alters nothing.

cards.front: A player fills one point of their own already-secure territory late in the game, capturing nothing. What happens to that player's score under area scoring, and under territory scoring?
cards.back: Under area scoring the score is unchanged: the point simply converts from a territory point to a stone point, and both count the same. Under territory scoring the score drops by one point: the point stops counting as territory and nothing is gained in its place, since no capture occurred.

cards.front: A 4 kyu player and a 9 kyu player want to play a handicap game under Japanese rules. How many stones, on which points, and what komi?
cards.back: The rank gap is five grades, so Black takes a five-stone handicap: the four corner hoshi plus tengen (the center point). Komi is the nominal handicap value, 0.5, not an even-game komi.

cards.front: A club is running a six-stone handicap game. A player new to handicap games assumes tengen must be one of the six points, since it appeared at five stones and will appear again at seven. Why is that assumption wrong?
cards.back: Tengen is not cumulative across handicap sizes. It is added at 5 stones, removed at 6 (replaced by the two side hoshi), added back at 7, removed again at 8 (replaced by the remaining two side hoshi), and added back at 9. At six stones the board holds the four corners plus two side points, with no stone on tengen.

cards.front: Why did the Nihon Ki-in raise Japanese-rules komi from 5.5 to 6.5 in 2002 instead of leaving it unchanged?
cards.back: Recorded results under the 5.5 komi showed Black winning about 51.855 percent of games, indicating the existing komi undercompensated for the first-move advantage. Raising komi to 6.5 was a direct response to that measured imbalance, not an arbitrary change.

cards.front: A tournament director running an event under Ing rules tells Black to "put the handicap stones wherever you like, not just on the hoshi." Is this an error?
cards.back: No. Ing rules, along with Chinese and New Zealand rules, permit free placement of handicap stones rather than requiring the fixed hoshi pattern. The Japanese fixed order is the common default, not a universal requirement.

cards.front: A player is 6 kyu and wants a handicap game against a friend who is 2 dan. How many handicap stones should the weaker player take?
cards.back: The ladder runs ...4 kyu, 3 kyu, 2 kyu, 1 kyu, 1 dan, 2 dan. From 6 kyu to 1 kyu is 5 grades, and from 1 kyu to 2 dan is 2 more grades (1 kyu to 1 dan, then 1 dan to 2 dan), for a total gap of 7 grades. The weaker player takes 7 handicap stones.

cards.front: A player holds a "5 kyu" account on one server and a "5 kyu" account on a different server, and loses most of their games when they use the second account against players who were also 5 kyu there. Does this mean the player's strength has gotten worse?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Ranks are calibrated to each server's own player pool, and different servers are documented to run their ladders at different overall strengths (Fox running informally weaker than KGS at the same numeral is one concrete example). A rank that transfers unchanged in label can still sit at a different real strength on a different server, so a losing record right after switching servers is often a calibration gap, not a skill decline, until enough games let that account's own rating settle.

cards.front: After ten games on a brand-new account, a player's rank has already moved by six grades, and then over the next two hundred games it moves by only two more. Is something wrong with the rating system?
cards.back: No. A new account starts with maximum rating uncertainty, so early games move the estimate a large amount as the system narrows down a wide range of plausible strength. As uncertainty shrinks with more games against well-established opponents, each additional result carries less new information and moves the rating less. Fast early movement followed by a slow, plateauing rate of change is exactly how an uncertainty-tracking rating system (Glicko/Glicko-2) is supposed to behave, not a sign of malfunction.

cards.front: A player has stopped improving quickly and is now winning about half of their ranked games. Should they be discouraged?
cards.back: No. A correctly calibrated rank, matched against opponents near that same rank, is expected to produce a win rate close to 50%, since an even game between equally strong players gives each side about a 50% chance of winning. Winning close to half your games is the signature of an accurate rank, not a sign of stalled progress. Sustained improvement will show up as the rank itself moving upward over time, not as the win rate at any single rank climbing toward 100%.

cards.front: Why does the simple ko rule fail to stop a triple ko, even though it reliably stops an ordinary single ko?
cards.back: Simple ko only forbids recreating the position from exactly one move-pair ago. A triple ko's repeating position last occurred three move-pairs earlier, well outside that one-move lookback, so the rule's test never triggers even though the same position keeps recurring.

cards.front: A move would recreate a board position that occurred earlier in the game, but the player to move next is the opposite of who was to move next at that earlier occurrence. Is the move legal under positional superko? Under situational superko?
cards.back: Illegal under positional superko, which bans any recurrence of the whole-board arrangement regardless of whose turn it is. Legal under situational superko, which only bans a recurrence when the same player is to move next — here the player to move is different, so situational superko does not object.

cards.front: Under Japanese rules, what happens if a triple ko appears and neither player is willing to break the cycle?
cards.back: The game is declared "no result" (void) rather than decided, and is typically replayed, since Japanese rules do not generalize the ko rule into a superko clause that would forbid the repeating move outright.

cards.front: Why does komi affect the end of the game rather than the start of the board position?
cards.back: Because komi is a score adjustment, not an extra stone or changed move rule. It offsets Black's first move by changing the final count, not by altering local tactical play.

cards.front: Why is handicap useful even though komi already exists?
cards.back: Because komi balances even games, while handicap balances games between players of different strength. They address different asymmetries.

cards.front: Why is a connected group usually stronger than the same stones scattered apart?
cards.back: Connected stones share liberties, defend each other, and can build eyes as one unit. Scattered stones can be cut apart and attacked separately.

cards.front: Why does the phrase "two eyes live" matter more than raw stone count?
cards.back: A group survives by preserving secure internal liberties, not by merely having many stones. Two proper eyes usually make capture impossible under ordinary play.

cards.front: In the two-group seki above, why does playing at either shared point immediately backfire on the player who plays it?
cards.back: Filling one shared liberty removes one of the mover's own last two liberties, dropping that group into atari with only the other shared point left. The opponent's group still has that same point as its own last liberty, so the opponent plays it and captures. Because the same backfire happens to whichever side moves first, both sides prefer to leave the two points alone indefinitely.

cards.front: Why can a single weakly connected diagonal stone turn a real-looking eye into a false eye?
cards.back: An eye on the edge is secure only if the defending color holds at least two of the diagonal points around it, not just the four orthogonal points. If one of those diagonals depends on a stone that can itself be captured, the opponent can remove that stone and gain a stone directly next to the eye point, which breaks the enclosure that made the point a protected liberty in the first place.

cards.front: Why does Weiqi LSP Constitution depend on Regression Positions?
cards.back: **Founding incident.** On 2026-08-19 — the same day [Regression Positions](./regression-positions.md) was authored — that document's own R9 diagram (the area-score worked example) and its `expected:` block briefly disagreed with each other during authoring: the diagram is the source of truth, and its stone counts, territory counts, and area scores must be *derivable* from it, not merely asserted beside it. The disagreement was caught only because a human re-derived the arithmetic by hand before the position was trusted as a kernel regression fixture — not because any automated process read the diagram, replayed or recomputed it, and checked the `expected:` block's numbers against that computation. No such process existed. `weiqi-kernel`'s own test suite (`apps/weiqi-kernel/test/scoring.test.mts`) now encodes R9 correctly, transcribed by hand a second time by a careful implementer — but the corpus document itself has no standing guarantee that its *next* edit won't reintroduce the same class of slip, silently, since nothing reads `regression-positions.md` and checks it against `weiqi-kernel` the way `weiqi-kernel`'s tests check themselves against it. This is exactly the gap `weiqi-lsp` exists to close, and it is the incident this record's board authorization (below) points to as concrete evidence for what the plan's own regression-corpus clause already anticipated in the abstract.

cards.front: Two players finish a game with no seki and no disputed dead stones. One count is done under Japanese territory rules, the other under Chinese area rules. Why should you expect the same player to win both counts?
cards.back: Because area scoring only adds the value of stones on the board on top of territory, and both players place roughly the same number of stones over the course of an ordinary game, including the dame-filling moves near the end. That extra value cancels out between the two players, so the margin between the two counting methods is usually zero or one point, not enough to flip the result outside unusual positions like seki or disputed dead stones.

cards.front: A group is in seki. Why might a Chinese-rules count and a Japanese-rules count disagree about the score even though neither player captured anything?
cards.back: Territory scoring gives no territory and no prisoners for a seki, since nothing was enclosed as territory and nothing was captured. Area scoring still counts every living stone in the seki as a point for its owner. If the two sides of the seki have an unequal number of stones, area scoring will show a different margin than territory scoring, even though the position and the set of living groups are identical under both rule sets.

cards.front: Why do New Zealand and Ing rules allow multi-stone suicide when Japanese, Chinese, and AGA rules forbid it, and why does this rarely matter in practice?
cards.back: New Zealand and Ing rules were written to remove the suicide prohibition as an unnecessary special case rather than because suicide is normally useful; a legal multi-stone suicide move only changes the outcome of a small number of unusual double-ko or capturing-race positions. Because those positions are rare, most games played under any of these five rulesets would end identically whether or not multi-stone suicide were legal.

cards.front: A beginner asks which ruleset they should learn first. What should they actually do, and why?
cards.back: Learn whichever ruleset their club, teacher, or server already uses, and stop worrying about the others. The differences between rulesets are almost entirely about how an already-finished position gets converted into a final score, not about how liberties, captures, or life and death work during play. A beginner's practical skills transfer completely across every ruleset described here.

cards.front: Why does area scoring depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Area scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the number of that player's own live stones remaining on the board plus the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md); captures made during play matter only insofar as they change which stones are on the board at the end, not as separately counted prisoner points [@britgo2025default]. Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules all use area scoring. Because a stone on the board and an enclosed empty point are worth the same one point each, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs nothing under area scoring: it simply converts a territory point into a stone point.

cards.front: Why does area scoring depend on Rulesets?
cards.back: That single property is the main practical difference from [territory-scoring](./territory-scoring.md), and it is why area-scoring rulesets can set standard [komi](./komi.md) a half-point to a full point higher than territory-scoring rulesets covering the same game: Black, moving first, typically ends a game with one more stone on the board than White, and area scoring counts that stone directly where territory scoring would not. The exact standard komi for each ruleset is recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).

cards.front: Why does dead stones depend on life and death?

cards.front: Why does dead stones depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Dead stones in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are stones left on the board after both players [pass](./pass.md) that cannot avoid eventual [capture](./capture.md) under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture [@britgo2026howtoplaygo]. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test [life-and-death](./life-and-death.md) reading always applies: it cannot make two secure [eyes](./eye.md) and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in [seki](./seki.md) and is never marked dead.

cards.front: Why does dead stones depend on Rulesets?
cards.back: How dead stones are settled is one of the sharpest procedural differences between rulesets, and one the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) records explicitly. Japanese-style rules settle status by mutual agreement after the two passes, which is fast but is the classic source of scoring disputes when players disagree about a group's fate [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Chinese-style area-scoring play resolves genuine disagreements by resuming alternating play until the disputed group is actually captured or clearly alive, which is slower but leaves no room for disagreement about the result.

cards.front: Why does hoshi depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Hoshi in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen [@wikipedia2026handicap]. The nine points sit at the 4-4 point in each corner, the 4-10 point on the midpoint of each edge, and the 10-10 point at the exact center of the board [@wikipedia2026handicap].

cards.front: Why does hoshi depend on Handicap Placement and Komi Values?
cards.back: Hoshi matter for two distinct reasons. First, they are the standard locations for handicap stones: the fixed Japanese placement pattern seats every handicap stone, from two up to nine, on one of these nine points, and the tengen point is the fifth and seventh stone added as handicaps increase (see [Handicap Placement and Komi Values](../../documents/articles/notes/handicap-placement-and-komi-values.md) for the full placement order). Second, even outside handicap games, the corner hoshi mark a natural opening frame: a stone on the 4-4 point does not by itself secure the corner the way a 3-3 point does, trading that immediate territory for speed and center-facing influence, which is why it is one of the most common corner openings for beginners to learn even though the 3-4 point (komoku) is usually described as the more evenly balanced choice between territory and influence [@nagofed2026thisisgo; @gomagic2026komoku].

cards.front: Why does pass depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: A pass in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent [@britgo2025default]. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by [ko](./ko.md), [suicide](./suicide.md), or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open [dead-stones](./dead-stones.md) settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture [@usgo2022agarules].

cards.front: Why does seki depend on life and death?
cards.back: Seki is the standoff outcome that arises specifically when neither side's life-and-death reading resolves in its favor.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on eye?
cards.back: Groups in seki characteristically lack the two eyes that would make them unconditionally alive.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on liberty?
cards.back: Seki is defined by a shared, unfillable pool of liberties between opposing groups.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on area scoring?
cards.back: Area scoring counts each seki group's own stones but not the shared liberties between them.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on territory scoring?
cards.back: Territory scoring credits neither side with the shared liberties inside a seki.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Seki in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a standoff in which two or more groups of opposite color share their remaining [liberties](./liberty.md), and neither side can play into the shared liberties without reducing its own group to a liberty count the opponent can then capture on the next move [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Neither group has two [eyes](./eye.md), yet neither can be captured either, so both remain on the board unresolved for the rest of the game. Seki is a genuine third outcome for a local fight, distinct from either group living outright or dying.

cards.front: Why does seki depend on Rulesets?
cards.back: Seki matters for scoring because it is handled differently, in detail, by different rulesets, which is exactly the kind of parameter the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md) exists to pin down. Under territory scoring, the shared liberties inside a seki count as points for neither player and stones in seki earn no prisoner value, since nothing was captured. Under area scoring, each side's own stones in the seki count as that side's area as normal, while the shared liberties still count for neither side, since they are not enclosed exclusively by one color.

cards.front: Why does suicide depend on liberty?

cards.front: Why does suicide depend on capture?
cards.back: A move is never suicide if it captures an opposing group first, since capture is checked before self-liberties.

cards.front: Why does suicide depend on eye?

cards.back: Ko recaptures and suicide are easy to confuse; ko always captures one stone, suicide by definition captures none.

cards.front: Why does suicide depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Suicide in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a move that would leave the moving player's own stone or group with zero [liberties](./liberty.md) after any opposing stones it removes are taken off the board [@britgo2025default]. Under most rulesets suicide is simply illegal: a player may not place a stone that reduces their own group to no liberties unless that same move first captures an opposing group and thereby restores at least one liberty. New Zealand rules are the well-known exception, permitting suicide of any size — a player may play a stone, or fill their own group's last liberties entirely, and the played stones are then immediately removed as self-captured [@nzgo2013rules].

cards.front: Why does superko depend on ko?
cards.back: Superko generalizes the simple ko rule from one forbidden position to all previously occurring positions.

cards.front: Why does superko depend on capture?
cards.back: Superko violations can only arise from sequences of captures and recaptures, since placement alone never restores an earlier board.

cards.front: Why does superko depend on liberty?
cards.back: Long ko cycles that superko must adjudicate arise from groups repeatedly reduced to and restored from a shared last liberty.

cards.front: Why does superko depend on seki?
cards.back: Some multi-ko fights that superko must resolve are closely related to seki: neither side can safely play the deciding capture.

cards.front: Why does superko depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Superko in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is a repetition rule that extends [ko](./ko.md) beyond the single immediately-preceding position: it forbids recreating *any* whole-board position that has already occurred in the game, not only the one position just before the opponent's last move [@britgo2025default]. Two variants are in common use. Positional superko (PSK) forbids any recurrence of an identical arrangement of stones, regardless of whose turn it is. Situational superko (SSK) forbids a recurrence only when it is also the same player's turn to move as it was the earlier time that arrangement occurred — so the same stone arrangement may legally recur once with the other player to move, but not a second time with the original player to move [@usgo2022agarules].

cards.front: Why does superko depend on Rulesets?
cards.back: Superko matters because the simple ko rule alone only blocks immediate two-move recaptures; it does nothing to stop longer cycles, such as triple ko or other multi-ko patterns, from repeating a board position indefinitely and preventing the game from ever concluding. Superko rules close that gap by treating repetition of the whole board, not just of one local point, as the thing to forbid. Which variant a ruleset adopts is one of the parameters recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md), since Chinese-tradition and New Zealand rules typically use positional superko while AGA rules specify situational superko, and Japanese rules historically rely on simple ko alone plus an ad hoc "no result" convention for unresolved long cycles.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on territory?
cards.back: Territory scoring's core term is the vacant points a player's stones enclose.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on area scoring?
cards.back: Territory scoring and area scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on komi?
cards.back: Standard komi values differ between territory-scoring and area-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on dead stones?
cards.back: Territory-scoring rulesets typically resolve dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on capture?
cards.back: Captures matter directly under territory scoring, since prisoners are added to the final count.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Territory scoring in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) computes each player's final score as the vacant points that count as that player's [territory](./territory.md) plus the prisoners that player captured from the opponent during the game; a live stone remaining on the board at the end contributes no direct point value of its own [@nihonkiin1989rules]. Japanese and Korean rules use territory scoring. Because stones themselves are not counted, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs a full point under territory scoring: it removes one territory point and, since nothing was captured, adds nothing back.

cards.front: Why does territory scoring depend on Rulesets?
cards.back: That cost is the main practical difference from [area-scoring](./area-scoring.md), and it is one reason experienced players under territory scoring stop playing inside their own territory as soon as a group is settled, while players under area scoring can fill such points for free. The exact standard komi and other parameters for each ruleset are recorded in the [rulesets comparison](../../documents/articles/notes/rulesets.md).

cards.front: Why does territory depend on liberty?
cards.back: Territory remains meaningful only if the surrounding stones retain enough liberties to hold it.

cards.front: Why does territory depend on capture?
cards.back: Captures can secure or destroy territory by changing which stones remain on the board.

cards.front: Why does territory depend on komi?
cards.back: Komi adjusts final scores after territory has been counted.

cards.front: Why does territory depend on ko?
cards.back: Ko fights can determine whether a key territorial area remains secure.

cards.front: Why does territory depend on Weiqi?
cards.back: Territory in [weiqi](../topics/weiqi.md) is the set of vacant points effectively enclosed by one player's stones and unavailable to the opponent except at unacceptable cost [@britannica2026go; @nagofed2026thisisgo].
